pages.title: Crypto From Scratch | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: What crypto does, and what it's worth
pages.description: What crypto is good for, what it is bad at, and why a coin has a price at all. Start from the beginning.
pages.text: Crypto from scratch What crypto does, and what it's worth Crypto earns its cost when strangers need one shared record of who owns what, and no single firm, bank, or state is trusted to keep it. Every other question, including price, comes back to that one job. The primitive A blockchain is a costly shared ledger One list of who owns what, kept by thousands of strangers at once, with no company, bank, or state holding the copy that counts. Every holder checks every new entry against the same rules, and changing an old entry means redoing the work behind everything after it. The marketing version NIST's definition Implies a token, a mining reward, and decentralization by default. Bitcoin, stablecoins, NFTs, DeFi, and smart contracts all get lumped in as if they were one thing. NIST IR 8202 defines a blockchain by four properties: hard to alter, tamper-evident, replicated across many holders, and typically leaderless. Nothing in that definition requires a token, a mining reward, or decentralization beyond copy count. Bitcoin, stablecoins, NFTs, DeFi, and smart contracts are all apps layered on that one narrow structure, not defined by it. Hide the eight eras Era Fix Mechanism Before Bitcoin Digital cash Faked the scarcity atoms have free. Bitcoin Double-spending PoW made rewriting payment history too costly to bother. Early mining Security market CPUs became ASICs, solo miners became warehouse farms. Litecoin and forks Parameter experiments Forked Bitcoin's code to change block time, algorithm, or scale. Ethereum Programmability A ledger that runs code, not just balances. 2017 ICOs and scaling war Fundraising outran products; Bitcoin split over how to scale. DeFi and stablecoins On-chain finance Dollar tokens and market makers turned demos into habit. Rollups and fast L1s Scale and UX Execution moved off the base chain into L2s and new L1s. That checking is the cost. Where the strangers really do need a record none of them controls, nothing cheaper does the job. Where one of them could simply run the database, a blockchain is a slower and more expensive way to reach the same list. Nobody can push an update to it either. Each operator running the software picks which rules to enforce, and a fork is what happens when they stop picking the same ones. Soft forks, hard forks, and the bets other projects made Soft-fork changes tighten the rules, so upgraded nodes enforce new limits while un-upgraded nodes still see those blocks as valid. Hard-fork changes break what old software accepts, sometimes planned and boring, sometimes the moment a chain splits in two. Bitcoin Cash split over block size. Ethereum traded Bitcoin's spare rule set for programmable state. Solana-style chains bought speed with hardware most people can't run. Monero and Zcash bought privacy with heavier math and legal heat, and stablecoins bet on an issuer or a collateral pool over a central bank. Kaspa kept PoW and UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. and swapped the single chain for a blockDAG. Kaspa's fair launch is what was left after DAGLabs and several hardware, presale, and business-model paths fell through; the origin page has the sourced version. Where crypto fits Where it wins, and where it loses Four places it does real work Bearer digital assets Whoever holds the private key controls the asset; an exchange freeze cannot touch a self-held coin. Cross-border settlement Stablecoins are flawed dollar tokens, still one of crypto's clearest wins: paid abroad in minutes, not days. Programmable escrow Smart contracts hold up when the test is plain: both sides signed, a vesting date arrived. Open-network incentives Tokens pay the validators and storage hosts an open network runs on, with no one firm hiring all of them. Four places it usually loses Payments at home Cards, Pix, UPI, SEPA, and Apple Pay beat crypto on refunds, fraud handling, and support. Ordinary databases If one owner already controls the users, data, and rules, a blockchain only adds cost to a solved problem. Anything a court settles Fraud, a wrong-address payment, a divorce, a stolen name: cases courts exist for, and code cannot reach them. Facts from the physical world A blockchain keeps whatever gets typed into it. Lie about where the tuna came from and the chain keeps the lie forever. "Trustless" is the wrong word. Crypto moves trust around: what you took from the bank teller lands on code, wallets, bridges, oracles, and law. Hide the tradeoff table Property Benefit Cost Self-custody You hold the keys yourself Lose keys, lose funds Irreversibility Final settlement Fraud is hard to undo Public ledger Transparency and auditability Privacy leakage Permissionless access Anyone can participate Scams and junk projects thrive Programmability Automated financial logic Smart-contract and oracle risk Decentralization No single operator Slower choices and worse UX Token incentives Bootstraps open networks Price bets and rewards that misfire Global settlement Cross-border access Rules differ in every country Market value Why a coin has a price, and what the number means A token price is smoke; the question is what's burning underneath it. Four things push it: someone needs the asset to pay fees, settle a trade, stake, or post collateral; scarcity people believe in; higher rewards buying more security; and reflexivity, price rising because people expect it to. Hide the five token roles Role What it does Beginner warning Thing being tracked The ledger defines and transfers the asset itself. A token can exist without being useful outside speculation. Fees Users pay for scarce block space and spam resistance. Low fees help UX but can weaken fee revenue or invite spam. Security budget Miners or validators need paying to defend the record. Rewards may come from inflation, fees, or both. Collateral Some systems require staked tokens or bonded assets. Stake-based security pools around big holders and custodians. Governance Some tokens vote on parameters, treasuries, or upgrades. Governance rights can be weak, captured, or mostly symbolic. Market cap is not company value Market cap is price times circulating supply, nothing more. That much cash never had to flow in, no revenue sits behind the number, and nobody could sell the whole supply at that price. One KAS costs less than one BTC simply because there are far more of them; compare market cap and liquidity instead of unit price. More numbers that mislead, and what open markets help and break Price per coin means nothing without supply attached, circulating supply can differ sharply from total supply, and a low float inflates paper valuations without matching real capital. Volume can mean liquidity, hype, wash trading, or panic. Fully diluted value shows the dilution still coming, and social dominance measures attention, not uptake. Markets help: miners and validators can sell rewards, apps can price collateral, and anyone can enter or exit without asking one issuer. Markets break: pump-and-dumps run easy, insiders use retail liquidity as exit liquidity, and leverage forces violent selling. Early buyers profiting in an open market does not make an asset a Ponzi. What does: a fixed promised return, yield paid from new deposits instead of income, or hidden insiders. Initial ownership shapes trust A fair launch removes the official allocation table, not the funding and early-miner questions a premine would have paid for. Kaspa mined its supply from zero: see that shape plotted against three chains that started with a premine or a sale . Hide the five launch models Launch model What it improves What it risks Fair launch / mined launch Lower official insider-allocation risk. No built-in treasury, early-miner advantage, harder funding. Premine Funds development, legal work, grants, audits, and integrations. Insider control, sell pressure, trust problems. Public sale or ICO Fast fundraising and broad early buyer base. Legal risk, hype buying, sloppy product work. VC allocation Real funding and business support. Unlock overhang and retail exit-liquidity risk. Airdrop Rewards users and spreads supply wider. Farming, sybil attacks, instant sell pressure. Rule: a price pump doesn't prove uptake, and a high market cap doesn't prove usefulness. A solid project can still be overpriced. Decision rule Crypto makes sense when at least three are true Tick what is true of whatever project you are weighing. The hardest one is not on the list: if the job is proving an off-chain fact is true, no ledger can do that for you. Shared ledger across parties that do not fully trust each other Users need to verify the rules themselves Assets must move globally, 24/7 Users need self-custody Users need censorship resistance The asset is digital or legally represented digitally Settlement speed is worth limited reversibility The product needs composability with on-chain systems A token is necessary to coordinate incentives Bridge to Kaspa Judge Kaspa where shared records need neutrality Kaspa's lane is narrow: proof of work, self-custody, global settlement, censorship resistance, fast confirmations, and later, apps that prove their own rules. Four mechanisms carry it. A blockDAG orders parallel blocks instead of making them race for one slot. The UTXO model settles who owns what. Mass rules price the compute and storage a transaction costs, not just its byte size. Covenants let a coin carry rules about how it can be spent next. Chainalysis 2024 Latin America report for stablecoin use in Argentina and Brazil. IMF Understanding Stablecoins for stablecoin policy risks. BIS Annual Economic Report 2025, Chapter III on tokenized money and the systems behind it. Securitize / PR Newswire on BUIDL surpassing $1B AUM , a dated mark for tokenized funds. BIS Annual Economic Report 2022, Chapter III for the case against crypto as a money system. Next Next: What is Kaspa? pages.title: What Is Kaspa? Proof-of-Work blockDAG Explained | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What is Kaspa? KAS, Proof of Work, blockDAGs, GHOSTDAG, 10 BPS, and what's live on mainnet versus still roadmap.
pages.text: Beginner answer What is Kaspa? Kaspa is a live proof-of-work blockDAG Blocks arrive in parallel and all of them are kept, so the record is a graph rather than a single line. network. Its native coin is KAS. The network keeps Bitcoin-style mining and UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. ownership, and GHOSTDAG orders parallel blocks into one payment history. Limits get their own page: Risks and Open Questions covers adoption, node load, and security budget. The core move Parallel blocks are the whole design A block takes time to reach the rest of the world. When blocks outrun that propagation, miners build on stale information and produce competing blocks a single chain can only keep one of. Bitcoin's answer is to make blocks rare, roughly one every ten minutes, so collisions stay rare too. Why rare blocks are the fix, and what it costs At a ten-minute interval, propagation delay is small next to the interval itself. Most blocks finish spreading before the next one is found, so a collision is a rare accident rather than routine, and Bitcoin never needed a rule for keeping both sides of one: discarding the loser is cheap enough. The cost lands on confirmation time instead. A payment needs several block intervals to be safe, which is why it settles at the pace it does rather than in seconds. How fast blocks are found: i Why the range stops at 32 32 a second is the top of this slider because it's the fastest rate GHOSTDAG has a configured margin for: rusty-kaspa's own k table stops at 32 and panics above it. Bitcoin, 1 every 10 min Kaspa mainnet, 10/s How long a block takes to reach other miners: i Why 250 ms, and what the slider's top end means The 250 ms default is bracketed, not measured directly. Walking 1,399 consecutive selected-parent chain blocks through api.kaspa.org (10,719 blocks, 24 August 2026) found 86.9% were concurrent blocks a strict one-winner chain would have discarded. Inverting that share on this model gives a single-chain-equivalent delay of roughly 204 ms to 666 ms, and 250 ms sits inside that range. A DAG's parallelism inflates the discard share past what a true single chain would show, so the range brackets the number without settling it. The slider's top end, 5 seconds, is NETWORK_DELAY_BOUND , rusty-kaspa's own one-way worst-case assumption, a protocol constant rather than a typical delay. i What this model is and how it was checked A Poisson single-chain race model, not an observation of any running network. Checked against real data: Decker & Wattenhofer measured Bitcoin's stale rate at 1.69%, with a mean propagation delay of 12.6 s. Solving this model backward for that stale rate gives about 10.3 s, the same order of magnitude as the measured figure, within roughly 1.5 to 2x. Not an exact match. The tally in the panel below is a running sample: it reads differently early on and drifts toward that figure as more blocks are produced. Each thrown-away block cost a miner real electricity and bought nothing. Single chain is a model, not a picture of Bitcoin today. Single chain so far: 0 kept, 0 thrown away kept, on the chain thrown away, off it BlockDAG so far: 0 kept, 0 thrown away every block kept, each pointing at the parents it saw Step one block How this works, and the sources Blocks arrive at random, a Poisson process with rate λ. A block collides with the one before it when the next block is found before the first has finished spreading, which takes time d. The chance of at least one collision is: p = 1 − e −λd (λ = block rate, d = propagation delay) That is not the share this demo reports. A single chain that has already kept a block rejects anything mined before that block finished spreading, so a run of collisions keeps only the first, the way a non-paralyzable dead-time counter drops events inside its recovery window. Working that through gives a lower share: discarded share = λd ÷ (1 + λd) kept share = 1 ÷ (1 + λd) Inferred from the identity above, matching this simulator's own discard rule rather than quoted from a source. At the opening settings λd = 2.51, so p works out to about 92% while the discarded share is about 72%. The running tally converges toward that second figure. A single chain can only keep one block per collision, so the loser's work is wasted. A blockDAG references every block a miner could see when it started working, so both survive and get ordered instead. Where this comes from. Poisson block creation at rate λ, with propagation delay as the cause of concurrent blocks, is the model in Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar's PHANTOM/GHOSTDAG paper ( eprint.iacr.org/2018/104 ): "Block creation follows a Poisson process with parameter λ," bounded by a network delay diameter D. Verified against that primary source. p = 1 − e −λd is the simpler building block underneath the paper's own anticone bound: standard Poisson math, P(0 arrivals in time d) = e −λd , and the same collision mechanism the Bitcoin fork-rate literature uses (Decker & Wattenhofer, Information Propagation in the Bitcoin Network , IEEE P2P 2013). Inferred from that identity, not quoted from either paper. This demo also tests only the immediately preceding block, not the full anticone GHOSTDAG resolves. Below one block a second the display runs faster than real time, by the factor named under the slider. From one block a second up it is real time. The collision math always uses the real rate and delay, never the playback speed. Kaspa keeps the fast blocks and fixes the order instead. A block points at every tip its miner could see, so two blocks found a moment apart both land in the record as parents of whatever gets mined next. The word blockDAG names that shape. GHOSTDAG reads the resulting graph and derives the order. Kaspa's origin story covers how that research reached mainnet. What you feel above is inclusion speed: mainnet makes ten blocks a second, so a broadcast transaction usually lands in a block within about a second. Inclusion is not settlement; the gap between them is what confirmations measure. Supply itself is capped on a fixed emission schedule with no premine. The ordering rule How GHOSTDAG turns a graph into one line Parents Every block names the tips its miner could see when it started hashing. Those references are the whole data structure. Coloring The k cap below decides color. Blocks that stay inside it join the blue set GHOSTDAG marks well-connected blocks blue and less-compatible ones red, for ordering and security accounting. ; the rest are marked red and keep their place, their parents, and their transactions. Spine Each block picks the parent carrying the most blue work Accumulated proof-of-work weight carried by blue blocks. It's how Kaspa compares competing DAG histories. as its selected parent The parent block that defines the main ordering path through the DAG. Not the same thing as Bitcoin's longest chain. . Chain those picks together and you get the closest thing Kaspa has to Bitcoin's longest chain. One order Walk that spine from genesis to the current tip, absorbing each mergeset The set of past blocks a new block pulls into view: how parallel work gets folded into the ordering. in turn with blue blocks ahead of red ones, and every block in the graph ends up in a single line. Miners don't take turns: independent miners publish blocks whenever they find them, so more than one can arrive at once. Advance time Or pick how many arrive at once: − 2 blocks + Mine this many Reset Advanced: hide blocks, then release them Publish nothing for a while and mine on your own, then bring your blocks back. The rest of the network doesn't wait for you. See what happens when it already moved on without you. Hide blocks Mine a secret block Release 0 Your blocks are hidden. No one else can see or build on them yet. The rest of the network is not waiting: it keeps mining and publishing while you stay hidden. Advanced: how forgiving the network is Every block can have some other blocks beside it that it never saw. This caps how many of those are still allowed to count. Lower it, and blocks get locked out sooner. Raise it, and more blocks keep counting even when a lot of them arrive at once. Uncounted neighbors allowed (k): 3 The block graph Scroll to see more → counted in the order locked out Hover or tap any block to see why. Show what the network sees Linear order The one ordering every node agrees on. i How this order is built Walk the main chain, and slot each block's counted neighbors in before its locked-out ones. Without one order every node agrees on, two people can each be told a different owner for the same coin. How the colors get decided Every block names the tips its miner could see when it was made, and those references are the whole data structure. A block's past is everything behind it, its future is everything built on top of it, and its anticone is everyone else: blocks that neither saw it nor were seen by it. Each block picks the parent with the most accumulated work as its selected parent, chaining block to block into a main chain. A block counts (blue) if the number of already-counted blocks in its anticone stays under the cap, k. Over the cap, it is locked out (red) instead. The DAG has no single "now": blocks keep arriving in parallel, with no one moment everyone agrees on. Kaspa's answer is the virtual block, a conceptual block that is never mined and never sent to anyone. It exists only on each node's own machine, standing in for everything that node has seen, and its parents, the virtual parents, are that node's current tips. Among those tips, the one with the most already-counted blocks behind it becomes the virtual selected parent, better known as the sink. That is the same rule an ordinary block uses to pick its own selected parent, applied one level up: to the node's whole view rather than to a single mined block. A block's anticone Blocks that sit in neither a block's past nor its future. Nodes need an anticone rule to order these consistently. is everything neither behind it nor built on it. A single chain has no way to rank an anticone, so it discards one side. GHOSTDAG ranks it instead, by one behavioral tell: an honest miner publishes a block the instant it is found, and a miner building a secret history does the opposite. Why honest and hidden miners produce different anticones Within a propagation delay, everyone else sees an honest miner's block and starts referencing it, so its anticone stays small by construction. Nobody can reference blocks they were never shown, so a hidden miner's withheld blocks surface later carrying wide anticones. An attacker's red blocks buy no weight in the accepted history, so the electricity behind them is wasted. Honest parallel blocks are kept instead of discarded, so running the block rate up does not burn the security budget on orphans the way it would on a single chain. Confirmations Fast is not final 1 Seen Your wallet broadcasts the transaction and nodes pick it up. 2 Included A miner mines it into a proof-of-work block. 3 Ordered GHOSTDAG places it against the blocks mined in parallel. 4 Accepted Nodes accept it under Kaspa's consensus rules. 5 Confidence Reversal risk keeps falling as more blocks stack proof-of-work on top of it. Kaspa has no single stack to count. Your block sits in a graph, and what piles up on it is blue work: the proof-of-work carried by every later blue block whose history includes yours. Reversal risk falls as that weight builds, which is why Kaspa publishes no universal confirmation count. How long before a payment is safe to trust prices the wait against an attacker of any size. What actually sets a safe wait, and how finality depth differs Undoing a payment means producing a competing set of blocks heavy enough to outweigh the one the network already accepted, and every new block referencing your transaction raises that bill. Wallets and explorers report the result as a confirmation count. At ten blocks a second Written 10 BPS in Kaspa's own documentation. Kaspa ran at one block a second until the Crescendo activation, DAA score 110,165,000, and has run at ten since. those references arrive quickly, so the risk curve drops steeply in the first seconds. Steeply is not vertically. Three things set the honest wait: the value at stake, hash rate now and how much it swings, and whether the payment can be undone outside the protocol. A shipping hold takes a thinner wait than handing over a good nobody can claw back. Exchanges and payment firms publish their own deposit rules, and those are the numbers a user meets. Finality depth The threshold past which old history counts as settled. is a different, deeper question: how far back the protocol will let anyone rewrite. It sits far past any payment wait, and once history is buried past it nodes reject a reorganization outright, which is also what makes pruning safe. Does pruning make Kaspa private? No. Pruning and missing explorer history are not privacy guarantees. UTXO state remains the consensus object, and a broadcast transaction can still be observed or archived by others before a node prunes it. Throughput Ask "TPS of what?" TPS is not one number. Kaspa mainnet makes ten blocks a second, and what fits in those blocks depends on what each transaction asks the network to do. A plain payment is cheap. A covenant or a proof is not. Four workload types, and why the TPS number moves Workload Answer Why the number changes Simple L1 payments About 2,450 TPS for a payment with change, 3,070 without. Set by the block rate and block-mass limits against simple transaction mass. Covenant or programmable L1 transactions Job by job, usually below simple-payment TPS. Covenants add script work, state rules, covenant IDs, extra outputs, and storage effects. ZK Zero-knowledge: a proof that a statement is true without revealing the data behind it, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without seeing that work. proof or settlement transactions Fewer, heavier L1 transactions. One proof or settlement transaction can carry many off-chain app actions. Set by the proof system, proof size, check cost, batch size, proving time, and settlement design. Effective ZK app or future vProg throughput App by app, and it can beat raw L1 transaction TPS. Count app actions per proof batch or settlement cycle. State access and prover work are the real limits. None of that makes throughput unlimited. A proof proves a statement about chosen inputs, so outside facts still need an anchor: a light client, finality certificate, reporter set, oracle, or challenge process. Build a transaction and see which mass dimension gets charged Kaspa charges a transaction for the room it takes, counted as mass Kaspa's own unit for how much block space a transaction uses. Not bytes, not KAS: the network charges a transaction for whichever kind of work costs it most, and only that one. , not bytes. Plain 1-in 1-out payment 1-in 2-out with change Covenant transaction ZK proof transaction Reset Build the transaction Inputs 1 Outputs 1 Amount per output (KAS) 1,000 This shape frees at least as much stored state as it creates, so its storage mass is 0 at any amount. Payload / proof bytes 0 Advanced: script per input Simple signature (1 signature check) Covenant / compute budget Compute budget units per input 50 How many fit in a block 0 transactions like this fit in a block 0 transactions per second at ten blocks a second, if every block were full of this shape. Change the shape and the count changes with it, which is why a headline transactions-per-second figure says nothing until someone names the transaction it counted. Three limits, each with its own budget. Fill a block with this transaction and they run down like this. The one that empties first sets the count above. Compute mass i What counts as compute mass Cost of running this transaction's signature and script checks. A block holds 500,000 mass units of it. 0 each · 0% Storage mass i What counts as storage mass Cost of new state this transaction leaves behind, such as a change output. A block holds 500,000 mass units of it. 0 each · 0% Transient mass i What counts as transient mass Cost of proof data attached to the transaction, cleared after the block that included it. A block holds 1,000,000 mass units of it, raised from 500,000 at Toccata. 0 each · 0% Show the mass formulas Transaction size size = 94 (fixed header: version, in/out counts, locktime, subnetwork id, gas, payload hash, payload length) + payload_bytes + inputs × (118 fixed bytes: outpoint 36, sig-script length field 8, signature script ~66, sequence 8; +2 if covenant/v1) + outputs × (52 fixed bytes (value 8, version 2, script-length field 8, P2PK-style script 34) + 34 per output, if that output carries a covenant id) Compute mass compute_mass = size × mass_per_tx_byte (1) + Σ(2 + output_script_len) × mass_per_script_pub_key_byte (10) + script_mass script_mass = inputs × 1 sigop × GRAMS_PER_SIGOP_COUNT_UNIT (1000) [simple] = inputs × compute_budget_units × GRAMS_PER_COMPUTE_BUDGET_UNIT (100) [covenant] Transient mass transient_mass = size × TRANSIENT_BYTE_TO_MASS_FACTOR (4) Storage mass ( KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. -0009) C = STORAGE_MASS_PARAMETER (1,000,000,000,000) utxo_plurality(output) = ceil((63 + script_bytes + 32 if covenant else 0) / 100) A P2PK-style output (script 34) has plurality 1. A covenant-carrying output (63 + 34 + 32 = 129 bytes) crosses the 100-byte unit and has plurality 2, which squares its weight below. storage_mass = max(0, outputs × plurality² × C / out_amount_sompi − inputs × C / in_amount_sompi) in_amount_sompi assumes no fee: total out value split evenly across inputs. Which dimension binds Compute and storage share a 500,000 block-mass limit; transient's limit is 1,000,000, so it is normalized to the same scale before comparison: transient_norm = transient_mass × 500,000/1,000,000. tx_mass = max(compute_mass, storage_mass, transient_norm) tx_per_block = floor(500,000 / tx_mass) TPS = tx_per_block × 10 blocks/second This models a standard Schnorr P2PK-style input/output shape and assumes value is conserved with no fee. Real network TPS is lower once relay policy, fee markets, and mempool behavior are added on top of this pure mass ceiling. Formulas verified against rusty-kaspa mass code , consensus params , and core constants . Offline calculator, no network requests. Where the payment numbers come from Kaspa mainnet makes ten blocks a second. Current mainnet params cap compute and storage block mass at 500,000, which gives a budget of 5,000,000 transaction mass per second before policy, fees, relay, storage shape, and real mempool behavior come in. A signed plain P2PK-style 1-input, 1-output payment costs roughly 1.6k mass by the code's careful math; add a change output and a 1-input, 2-output payment runs closer to 2.0k mass. Divide the block budget by those shapes and the count lands around 250 to 300 simple transactions per block, about 2,450 to 3,070 per second at ten blocks a second. Leaner shapes and rounding push the top end to the often-quoted 3.4k TPS. Benchmarks built on fake minimum-size transactions score higher than that, and what they measure is a lab ceiling. Anything that makes a transaction bigger, from extra outputs to covenant metadata to proof bytes, crowds out the simple transfers competing for the same budget. Kaspa's docs put the payload ceiling around 25 KB when payload data dominates a standard transaction, because the standard transaction mass ceiling and transient byte accounting still apply on top of it. Toccata leaves the payment limit alone. Transient mass rises from 500,000 to 1,000,000 at activation while the compute and storage reference limit holds at 500,000, and the Toccata guide ties that rise to fitting STARK-sized proofs. Toccata also adds v1 transaction fields such as output covenant data and input compute commitments, and raises the standard minimum relay fee. It is mostly an upgrade to what L1 transactions can say and check. Piece What it adds TPS implication KIP-17 covenants Transaction introspection and script tools for stateful UTXO rules. More expressive transactions run heavier than simple payments. KIP-20 covenant IDs A 32-byte covenant identifier that gives covenant state a lineage. Backs asset rules, at the cost of extra data and checking work. KIP-16 ZK precompile OpZkPrecompile for proof paths such as Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct. Proof transactions spend L1 room on checking work. Little of that room goes to moving coins. KIP-21 sequencing commitments Partitioned lane commitments. Cuts app proving cost. It is not itself an end-user TPS number. vProgs remain roadmap architecture. Toccata ships the parts vProg-style systems need without shipping vProgs. KIP-21 stops every prover from having to follow the whole DAG for every app: its partitioned commitment design targets O(activity) proving, so a prover for one app lane tracks only that lane. Current params cap user-lane churn at 50 non-coinbase lanes per block and 1,000,000,000 gas per lane, which at ten blocks a second is a worst-case 500 user-lane updates per second. User transaction throughput still needs its own transaction-shape math on top. The public kaspanet/vprogs repo shows where the build is headed. Michael Sutton A core Kaspa developer who led the Rust rewrite and much of 2026's covenant and scripting work, including Argent and Silverscript. 's Argent is an actor-based language and compiler that already builds multi-contract covenant apps into Silverscript A higher-level language that compiles down to Kaspa script, so a covenant can be written as readable rules instead of hand-assembled opcodes. , with an audit as the gate its README sets before real use. Covenants A coin that can carry its own rule Since Toccata went live at DAA score 474,165,565, a Kaspa coin can carry a rule about how it may move next. The network checks that rule the same way it checks a signature: a vault can ask for a delay and a backup key, an escrow a release or a refund. What Toccata turned on, KIP by KIP KIP-17 A UTXO can read the transaction spending it and require a matching next output: vaults, escrow, spend caps, refunds. KIP-20 Covenant IDs give covenant state a lineage consensus tracks, blocking fake lookalikes. KIP-16 A script checks a proof from a chosen proof system, initially Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct, instead of L1 running every app step itself. KIP-21 Sequencing commitments let an app prove its own lane instead of almost the whole DAG. vProgs Not part of what activated. Full vProgs, for shared app state many users mutate at once, are still roadmap architecture. See status . Based apps Apps anchor state to Kaspa ordering and settle proofs back to it, with no separate sequencer. No virtual machine, no accounts, no global shared state. App logic lives in bounded UTXO steps or proofs. A live demo that tries to break a covenant vault is on build on Kaspa . Primary sources: KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-16 , KIP-21 , and Michael Sutton's Toccata hard-fork outlook . Live vs next What's live, what's not Six claims checked against mainnet Claim Status Safer wording Kaspa is proof of work at ten blocks a second, ordered by GHOSTDAG Live All three describe current mainnet in the Crescendo era. Toccata has activated on mainnet Activated Toccata crossed its mainnet activation score. That protocol switch is live; app, wallet, explorer, and SDK support still need their own checks. July 2026 is a sudden emission cliff Misleading Emission steps down once a month, keyed to DAA score. The calendar has nothing to do with it. July 2026 sits inside one of those scheduled steps. GHOSTDAG is DAGKnight, or DAGKnight is current mainnet consensus Research DAGKnight is a separate, later consensus design, still research and implementation work. Current mainnet consensus runs GHOSTDAG. Ten blocks a second means payments are final immediately No The block rate is live and speeds up inclusion. Reversal risk falls as proof-of-work stacks up, so a recipient waits for the depth the amount at stake deserves. The blockDAG means unlimited TPS No Throughput is bounded by block capacity, mempool policy, fees, and demand. Anything not listed here goes through the claim fact-check , which sorts a claim into live, testnet, targeted, roadmap, research, wrong, unsupported, or out of scope. Sources Check it yourself Kaspa Research carries the protocol lineage; Rusty Kaspa is the code that runs it, including k and the rest of the consensus parameters. Kaspa.com's Learn Kaspa has term-by-term references for anticone, mergeset, and blue work: vocabulary and mechanics, not protocol status. Watch the network: a live read of Kaspa's own public API, not a simulation Real blocks, read live from Kaspa's own public API. i How often this reads, and what happens if it fails Kaspa makes about ten blocks a second; this checks in every 9 seconds and shows what it actually fetched, not a simulation of the rest. If the API can't be reached, it says so instead of faking it. Can't reach the public network right now. Retrying every 9 seconds. The explanation below still applies; nothing on this page is invented while it waits. 0 blocks racing for the same spot right now. Kaspa doesn't make them wait in line. Measuring the network's real pace… Reading the first blocks… Pause Checking every 9 seconds. 0% of the blocks this page has watched this session carried nothing but the miner's own reward. i How this compares to Kaspa's measured baseline Kaspa's own measured baseline runs the same way: about 0.9 transactions per second, and 88.3% of its raw transaction count is coinbase, one per block (site data, read from api.kaspa.org, 2026‑08‑22). An empty block is not a fault. The network makes room for ten a second whether anyone fills it or not, and most of that room goes unused. What this page shows, what it can't, and why What the count is The tip count at the top is tipHashes from a live read of api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag : how many block tips the network is holding open right now. Each new tip is then fetched from api.kaspa.org/blocks/{blockId} . A sample, not the whole feed The API sits behind an 8-second edge cache, so this page checks every 9 seconds. Kaspa makes roughly ten blocks a second in that gap, so each check catches a handful of them, not all. The line above the feed states both numbers. Miner names are self-reported The payout address and miner tag come from the block's own coinbase data ( extra.minerAddress and extra.minerInfo ). Neither is a verified identity: a pool can rotate addresses, and the tag is a plain string the miner chose to write. Red blocks are real blocks A block tagged red was mined honestly but arrived too late in its local ordering to count in the accepted history. Keeping the block and deciding whether it counts is GHOSTDAG's job. Empty blocks are real usage A block carrying only its own coinbase transaction is marked Empty , and most arrive that way. That is Kaspa's current usage, not a failed read. Tags are read, never inferred A covenant tag means the API returned a network-verified covenantId ; build-on-kaspa counts how many are running. An app: ciph_msg pill means the payload literally starts with that string. Anything else stays unlabeled rather than guessed. A ZK opcode call is not shown at all, because the REST API returns transaction scripts as opaque hex rather than decoded opcodes. What an explorer has that this does not Miner leaderboards, address balances and historical charts need a database of stored history. This page has one API read per visit, so it shows what that read contains. Endpoints: api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag (tip hashes and blockCount , polled every 9 seconds) and api.kaspa.org/blocks/{blockId} (one call per newly seen tip, capped at 16 per check). API surface: api.kaspa.org/openapi.json . Baseline throughput and coinbase-share figures: this site's data/l1-chains.json , cross-checked against live reads on 2026-08-22. Independent read of Kaspa's public API. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is stored or sent anywhere. Primary implementation and protocol references: rusty-kaspa params , rusty-kaspa mass code , wallet mass code , Toccata guide , v2.0.0 activation release , v2.0.1 maintenance release , KIP-16 , KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-21 , Kaspa programmability docs , transaction payload docs , kaspanet/vprogs , and argent-lang/argent .
