pages.title: Kaspa Design Case | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What Kaspa is trying to be: money nobody can quietly change the rules on, that still settles fast.
pages.text: Kaspa's design case Answer Crypto earns its keep when people need one shared record and no single operator running it. Kaspa's bet: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work Miners spend real computation to propose blocks. security can run closer to real time, without trading away censorship resistance for the speed. Start with the job Job Angle Status Self-custodied money Fair-launched Proof-of-Work UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. asset with wallet control. Live Fast payment feel Ten blocks a second, in a blockDAG A graph where multiple honest blocks exist in parallel instead of a single forced line. , beats a single-chain PoW block time. Live, with confirmation tradeoffs One shared record GHOSTDAG orders parallel honest blocks in a DAG. Live Assets with rules Toccata put spend rules, ZK hooks, sequencing commitments, and vProgs groundwork on-chain. Covenant rules live on L1; wallet and app evidence next. See Programmability, below . Group commitments Base Real-Time Decentralization (RTD) today; TangVM A proposed add-on, not yet built, that would let a smart contract watch outside data and trigger itself instead of waiting for someone to trigger it by hand. and attestations later. Base idea live; app systems still future work Why a public chain can't just be Visa-fast Visa settles fast because nobody outside Visa has to check its work: banks, contracts, one company's servers, and a fraud team handle that internally, and Visa can undo errors, block users, and change the rules at will. A public chain asks thousands of strangers to check the same rules, with no one in charge, so independent nodes can throw out bad history without asking anyone. That is the slow part. The app layer can be Visa-fast; a base layer anyone can check cannot. Concentration arrives by a different door in each model. ASIC cost gathers around whoever has the capital, the cheap power, and the chips. Proof of stake skips the hardware, so holding the token buys the say instead. Every one of those costs still lands on Kaspa. The bet it makes against them is narrow, and it starts with keeping the blocks that lose the race. Rare combination What the other networks are already good at Bitcoin has the longest track record as a store of value. Ethereum has the deepest pool of smart contracts. Solana has the most polished fast-app feel. Kaspa leads on none of the three today; its claim is a combination none of them make: mined issuance, fixed supply, blocks that arrive in parallel, and app rules on that same base layer. A paragraph can't rank them honestly; the chain comparer does, scoring twenty layer ones, family by family, on fields measured the same day. Pick your constraint Every design pays for its wins somewhere No crypto design gets speed, security, privacy, and a network nobody controls. Push on one and the cost lands somewhere else. Goal Why people want it What it costs Decentralization No easy single control point. Harder upgrades, worse UX, slower agreement, more on you. Security Hard-to-fake history and valid supply. Fees, power bills, staked capital, and a security budget that holds up. Speed Fast inclusion and better user feedback. Blocks clash more, nodes get heavier, checks thin out, control narrows. Privacy Less watching. Every coin spends the same. Heavier math, bigger data, harder to audit, fewer exchanges. Self-custody You hold the keys. No company account. No password reset, no chargeback, no support line. Latency, inclusion, and confirmation Bitcoin proved strangers can agree on scarce digital money with nobody in charge. It pays for that with a slow block interval, picked partly because network lag has to stay small next to block production. Kaspa comes out of the research line asking whether mining work that a single chain throws away as a collision can count toward consensus instead. Any fast block-producing system can get a transaction into a block quickly. That's inclusion. It says nothing about confirmation: how fast the network gives strong confidence the transaction won't reverse. Mixing the two up is the most common way "fast blockchain" claims mislead. How GHOSTDAG and real-time decentralization work Every Nakamoto-style system carries Bitcoin's latency tradeoff by design. RTD Hashdag's framing: Bitcoin-style PoW security operating in real time. , Real-Time Decentralization, is Hashdag Kaspa co-founder Yonatan Sompolinsky's research writing site, where he lays out design ideas ahead of protocol work. 's term for a partially synchronous system that moves as fast as the network really allows: fast when conditions are clean, slower but still safe when the network is struggling or under attack. Blue work is what makes it measurable, letting nodes compare total work across a graph instead of a single chain. See how GHOSTDAG colors and orders that graph and try the live version there. Storage-mass pricing charges a transaction for the UTXO footprint it leaves behind for good, on top of its raw size. Pruning and bounded anticones cap what a node has to hold and how far the parallel edges can spread, which is what lets an ordinary machine keep up with a fast proof-of-work DAG. Hashdag points that speed at shared commitments instead of price charts. The simplest version is Kickstarter-like funding, where money moves only if enough people commit and a public rule holds the threshold instead of a company that can wave it away. How Bitcoin, Kaspa, Ethereum, and Solana split on this Proof of Stake usually gets fast finality by quickly counting votes from staked validators, which ties confirmation speed to how well those validators coordinate and how the stake is spread. On Solana a stake-weighted schedule picks which validator leads each slot and puts the transactions in order. Push decentralization further and that job gets harder, which often drives the system toward committees or other sampling shortcuts. Proof of Work samples security a different way. A block is proof the finder beat the rest of the network's hash power for that round, so the protocol never has to poll most of the miners before it confirms anything. Block speed and miner headcount come apart. The two models also split on cost. Proof of Work brings outside cost into consensus, in power bills and hardware. Proof of Stake backs the ledger with token ownership inside the system instead. That gap changes who can censor, how new coins are issued, and what an attack costs. The block rate by itself is not the claim. K, finality depth, and merge depth all scale with it, and they are what keep high block production from turning into runaway parallelism. less stake-vote coordination Bitcoin slow inclusion, PoW confirmations Kaspa fast inclusion, PoW confirmations Ethereum PoS finality, committee sampling Solana fast UX, stake-vote finality faster inclusion Try it How long before a payment is safe to trust A payment already sitting in a block can still be undone. Waiting is what closes that window, and the block count is not what measures it. How much mining power the attacker controls: weak, 1% past the 50% line, 60% how careful you want to be i What a reorg does A reorg is not paperwork. If the block carrying your payment gets replaced, the attacker can spend the same coins again elsewhere. That double-spend is what this wait protects against. relaxed normal strict i What "safe" means, and what's on this chart Safe means the attacker has lost the race to out-mine your payment, a chance that falls the longer you wait. Kaspa's separate finality rule blocks any reorg past 432,000 blocks (12 hours), no matter the attacker's share; how the two differ is in the model details below. Three chains, same three this site compares everywhere: Bitcoin and Litecoin as classic single-chain proof of work at different speeds, Kaspa as the fast blockDAG this site explains. Modeled from the Bitcoin whitepaper's confirmation-risk formula, not a live network feed. The model, and where the Kaspa line is an approximation Model. This is the "double-spend race" from Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin whitepaper, section 11 (2008). An attacker holding a share of the network's mining power races to out-produce the blocks already confirming a payment. The whitepaper models that race as a Poisson process and asks: what is the chance the attacker still catches up after z blocks. P(z) = 1 − ∑ k=0 z Poisson(k; λ)·(1 − (q/p) z−k ), λ=z·q/p, q

pages.title: Why Parallel Spends Don't Collide | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Send five payments at once on a coin ledger and on a balance ledger, and watch which one has to take turns. Plus what the missing shared slot costs Kaspa apps.
pages.text: Two ledger models Why parallel spends don't collide An account balance is one number every payment has to take a turn writing. A UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. wallet holds separate coins, so nobody takes a turn. Try it Five payments, one moment Same 1,650 KAS, same five payments, two ways of keeping the books. Account model 1,650 one balance, in KAS UTXO model (Kaspa) Watch the five checks run Aim payment 5 at the coin payment 1 spends Kaspa targets ten blocks a second, so those five payments can land in five different blocks, in any order. Separate coins make the order irrelevant. One shared balance has to pick one, and four payments wait. Which spend wins, and who decides Nothing stops a wallet signing two spends of one coin and broadcasting both. The network does not refuse them at broadcast; it refuses to keep both. A single block cannot carry two spends of the same coin: rusty-kaspa turns that block down outright. The usual race is between two blocks landing at once. GHOSTDAG puts every block in one order first, then replays each block's spends against the running set of unspent coins. Whichever spend comes earlier in that order takes the coin. The later one fails and is never kept, while the block carrying it stays in the DAG and stays valid. Every node runs that rule over the same DAG and reaches the same answer, with no voting round. Whole coin in, change coin out: rusty-kaspa, consensus/core/src/tx.rs . An input names a whole prior output; an output carries a value and an optional covenant binding. One block cannot double-spend: block body validation . Order first, then replay: the mergeset acceptance loop . The demo models outpoint contention and account sequencing. It does not model mempool spread, block timing, or fee markets. The cost Nothing is locked because nothing is shared That cuts both ways. A Kaspa script reads the spend it sits in and nothing else. It cannot call another app's live state the way one contract calls another on an account chain, which is why broad contract platforms grew up on the account model first. So Kaspa's app layer is covenants A rule attached to a coin, checked by the network on every spend, about how that coin and the coins it makes are allowed to move. , not an account-based virtual machine. Three rungs, and only the first is running: What it does How far it reaches Status Covenants, covenant IDs, ZK proof checks Rules the network enforces on the one spend being checked. Live on mainnet since Toccata, at DAA score 474,165,565 Two separately built apps in one transaction Both apps are spent and remade together, so both land or neither does. Demos only unaudited and offline, in Argent Many users writing one app's state An order book or a pool that everyone edits at once. Roadmap vProgs, zero releases What each of the three rungs actually is KIP-17 gives a script check opcodes over the spend it sits in: that spend's own inputs, outputs and payload, not another spend's. KIP-20 adds covenant IDs, a lineage tag consensus tracks. An output can carry one only by continuing a covenant or starting a fresh one, so a covenant's record cannot be forged. KIP-16 adds an opcode that checks a zero-knowledge proof inside a spend, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without replaying it. None of the three lets a script read another covenant's live state. Argent's Inter-Covenant Communication composes apps by putting both apps' state in one spend's inputs and outputs, so one app's actor can authorize another's. Its own README calls the project "still under active development and is not yet release-ready." vProgs targets the case the other two do not reach, many users mutating one app's state. Its README opens: "This repository is in early development / prototype phase." Zero releases, zero tags. Michael Sutton frames the design choice as "losing synchronous composability or losing sovereignty." KIP-17, covenants and scripting , KIP-20, covenant IDs , KIP-16, the ZK verifier opcode , all Active on this site's KIP tracker . Toccata activation: rusty-kaspa v2.0.0 . argent-lang/argent , and what the compiler does . kaspanet/vprogs and Michael Sutton's design notes . Status labels on this site are checked against mainnet and releases: the claim fact-check . Next Next: Kaspa current status Every feature and repeated claim, labeled live, testnet, roadmap, research, or wrong, with the source behind each label.

pages.title: Kaspa Status | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What is live, targeted, roadmap, and research on Kaspa right now, checked against mainnet, releases, and KIPs.
pages.text: Current status Kaspa current status Live on mainnet right now Proof-of-work GHOSTDAG consensus, ten blocks a second since Crescendo The May 2025 upgrade that took Kaspa's mainnet from one block a second to ten. , and Toccata The mainnet upgrade activated 30 June 2026 that let a coin carry enforceable spending rules, called covenants, instead of just moving from one address to another. 's spend rules, asset rules, ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments. Not built yet DAGKnight is KIP-2 , still Proposed. GHOSTDAG runs consensus today. vProgs have not reached testnet. Argent's inter-covenant communication Separately compiled covenant apps joined into one all-or-nothing transaction, so either every part lands or none does. It works on Toccata today, in unaudited offline demos only. already composes covenant apps atomically on Toccata, in unaudited offline demos. What vProgs would add on top is shared mutable state, the case where many users change one app's state at once. Find a feature or a claim All Live Testnet only Roadmap Research Wrong What each status label means Label What it means here Live Running on Kaspa mainnet right now, backed by code, a release, or protocol docs. Testnet only Proved on a test network. That is not evidence of mainnet behavior. Roadmap Planned work with no committed activation date. Research Design or architecture work with no live or testnet proof yet. Wrong A claim people repeat that the sources contradict. Status What Kaspa has, and what it does not Checked 22 August 2026 against release tags, raw KIP and KCC files, and project READMEs. The L1 snapshot row was re-read from the network on 29 August 2026. Features and upgrades Feature Status Meaning Source Proof of work Live Kaspa runs on proof-of-work mining. Work and new coins never depend on a list of validators. rusty-kaspa UTXO model Live Kaspa tracks spendable outputs, the same model Bitcoin uses. Ethereum tracks balances instead. rusty-kaspa GHOSTDAG Live GHOSTDAG keeps blocks that lose the race to be first, instead of throwing them out. It then orders every kept block into one history. Kaspa Research , Research Q&A Crescendo, ten blocks a second Live Roughly 8 to 9 times the throughput and about 30% faster confirmations. It is not instant finality. Sutton's numbers, and the claim that overshoots them Michael Sutton A core Kaspa developer who led the Rust rewrite and much of 2026's covenant and scripting work, including Argent and Silverscript. put the throughput gain at roughly 8 to 9 times and the confirmation-time gain around 30%. A flat "10x faster confirmations" claim goes past his own numbers. releases ; Crescendo roadmap note L1 snapshot, 29 August 2026 Live Virtual DAA score 526,073,404, about 27.669 billion KAS in supply, 2.31246515 KAS per block, from a synced v2.0.1 node. One read at one moment, and what to skip The DAA score climbs about ten a second, so two reads minutes apart differ. Recheck before quoting it. Skip the block and header counts from this endpoint: it spreads reads across backend nodes with different pruning states, so the figure covers only the node that answered. Two reads a minute apart on August 8 returned 1,488,846 and 26,573,222. blockDAG API ; supply API ; block reward API ; explorer Emission schedule Live Steps down about 5.61% every 30 days, 23.12465141 KAS a second in this step. A block counter triggers each step, not the calendar. The steps, and why the dates drift Emission steps down every 2,629,800 seconds by a factor of 2 -1/12 , 426 steps deep in the consensus table. It ran 25.95654359 KAS a second at DAA 452,313,000, then 24.49971474 at 478,611,000, then 23.12465141 at 504,909,000, where the network sits now. That step fired around 5 August 2026, and the block reward API moved with it from 2.44997148 to 2.31246515 KAS a block. Next is 21.82676446 at 531,207,000, roughly 4 September 2026. Calendar dates drift because they depend on how fast blocks land. The DAA triggers do not. No month is a cliff. coinbase.rs subsidy table ; Kaspa Wiki tokenomics Toccata Live Hard fork for L1 spend rules, asset rules, Silverscript A higher-level language that compiles down to Kaspa script, so a covenant can be written as readable rules instead of hand-assembled opcodes. , ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments. Activated at DAA score 474,165,565, around 30 June 2026. Activation record v2.0.0 published 5 June 2026 as the mainnet Toccata release, setting activation at DAA score 474,165,565. v2.0.1 followed on 15 June 2026 as the maintenance release, adding standalone based-zk apps and vProgs groundwork. v2.0.1 ; v2.0.0 ; Toccata guide Base RTD framing Live Real-time decentralization is Hashdag Kaspa co-founder Yonatan Sompolinsky's research writing site, where he lays out design ideas ahead of protocol work. 's name for Kaspa's core trade: Bitcoin-style proof-of-work security with confirmations that feel seconds-scale on a normal network. hashd.ag/raw vProgs Roadmap Apps that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering. L1 never becomes one global machine that runs everything. vProgs repo ; programmability docs Native DeFi Roadmap A design target that follows the Toccata-era foundations. A live Kaspa-native app layer needs shipped apps and real usage. Design case DAGKnight Research A parameterless consensus direction, meaning it adapts instead of being tuned by hand. It does not run mainnet today. GHOSTDAG does. KIP-2 , still Proposed; hashd.ag 100 blocks a second, netsplit-resilient Describes a payment that would keep confirming correctly even if part of the network loses contact with the rest, a break called a netsplit. payments Research A proposed 2027 hard fork target: 10-millisecond blocks and netsplit-resilient local payments. No spec, code, or release exists. No anchor source. The only place this appears is a kaspa.org roadmap page, which this site does not accept as a source . RTD-derived oracles, TangVM A proposed add-on, not yet built, that would let a smart contract watch outside data and trigger itself instead of waiting for someone to trigger it by hand. Research Apps can build oracle, attestation, and coordination-market systems on top of Kaspa. The protocol ships none of them as products. hashd.ag/raw Claims people repeat Claim Verdict Evidence Kaspa is proof-of-work Live What the code says Kaspa is mined, proof-of-work, full stop. Source: rusty-kaspa . Kaspa is a blockDAG using GHOSTDAG Live What GHOSTDAG does GHOSTDAG orders parallel blocks into one history instead of discarding the losers. Source: the GHOSTDAG walkthrough . Kaspa produces ten blocks a second Live Where the rate is set Ten blocks a second, the Crescendo-era rate. Source: releases . Kaspa already runs at 100 blocks a second Research Why not Ten is live. A hundred is an unconfirmed roadmap proposal with no release, KIP, or code behind it. It exists only in kaspa.org's roadmap prose, which this site stopped citing after that page described Toccata as pre-mainnet eight weeks after activation. Kaspa payments become irreversible immediately Wrong What actually happens Inclusion is fast. Confidence in a confirmation rises over time rather than switching on. Source: the confirmation-risk demo . Toccata has activated on mainnet Live The activation record Activated at DAA score 474,165,565; v2.0.1 followed as the release. App, wallet, explorer, SDK, and user adoption are separate, still-open checks. Source: the feature table above . The TN10 Testnet-10, one of Kaspa's test networks, where upgrades get tried out before they reach the live mainnet. Toccata test is what activated mainnet Testnet only Why not No. tn10-toc2, tn10-toc3, and the Testnet-10 DAA evidence are testnet-only. v2.0.0 set the mainnet activation score. Source: v2.0.0 . TN12 Testnet-12, a separate Kaspa test network used the same way as TN10: trying out changes before mainnet. proves mainnet covenants Testnet only What actually proves it Covenants are live on mainnet, but TN12 is not why. That rests on the v2.0.0 activation score. TN12 is prototyping evidence. Kaspa has mature native smart contracts Not yet What is still ahead Toccata shipped the covenant and proof-check layer only. Mature native DeFi and full app infrastructure are still ahead, through later vProgs work. The three rungs on the UTXO page separate what Toccata put live from what vProgs would add. July 2026 was a sudden emission cliff Misleading What the schedule does Emission steps down by a fixed factor every 2,629,800 seconds, and the DAA score triggers the step rather than the calendar. It went 24.49971474 KAS a second from DAA 478,611,000, then 23.12465141 from 504,909,000, which the network passed around 5 August, then 21.82676446 from 531,207,000, roughly early September. Source: tokenomics . KCC-0020 A Kaspa Call for Conventions: a proposal for how different Kaspa wallets and apps can agree on a shared format, like a token standard. It does not change Kaspa's consensus rules; a KIP does that. is a ratified fungible-token standard Not yet The defect, and the one production implementer KCC-0001, KCC-0002, and KCC-0020 merged into the kccs repo, but each still reads Status: Draft in its own body. KCC-0020 also carries a permanent-supply-split consequence, issue #14: its transfer-consolidation rule and its extended-state update entrypoint contradict each other, so a token using the extended-state path can permanently split its own supply. Co-authors defend one pattern behind this as intended, a frozen or blacklist flag. They conceded a second pattern, ephemeral state that mutates without affecting fungibility, is a wrong one needing a spec fix. The issue remains open with no spec edit. KaspaCom, the one production implementer on record, calls its own deployed artifact partially aligned rather than fully conforming. Source: kccs repo . KCC-0021 and KCC-0402 are adopted standards already running in production Wrong Why not Both are open, unmerged pull requests. Neither is a merged spec. Their PR bodies claim production use, and those claims live inside the open proposals themselves and could not be independently confirmed. Source: kccs repo . DAGKnight is current mainnet consensus Research Where the branch stands No. Mainnet ordering runs GHOSTDAG. DAGKnight has a paper and a prototype branch, and the branch is active, with commits as recent as 14 August 2026 promoting its Universal Merge Consensus work. What it does not have is a merge: KIP-2 still reads Status: Proposed . Source: KIP-2 raw file . vProgs have shipped as production app infrastructure Roadmap What the repo shows instead No. Zero releases, zero tags, and the repo calls itself early development. Its tn10-flow example runs against a private testnet-10 fork node, separate from the public one. Source: vprogs repo . Argent proves Kaspa smart contracts are production-ready Research What the README claims is present No audit yet, and nothing has run on mainnet. Argent's own README says the main pieces are present: compiler, generated Silverscript, portable artifacts, runtime transaction building, multi-actor routing, and closed and open ICC. Silverscript has to finish its own audit first, then Argent needs hardening of its own. Source: Argent README . Native DeFi has shipped as a mature Kaspa L1 product layer Roadmap The covenant numbers behind that verdict Genuine early usage at small scale, with lending still absent from mainnet. Kaskad and Igra-style L2 lending is ecosystem context around Kaspa, separate from native L1 DeFi. See build-on-kaspa for current covenant counts and value; that figure moves fast enough that this page does not restate it. No feature or claim matches that. Try a broader word like Toccata , DAGKnight , emission , or covenant , or press All. Evidence The code behind each label Every label above traces to a repository, a release, or a proposal file. This is that trail, one row per track. Eight tracks: what exists in public, and how to read it Track What exists in public How to read it Toccata and Silverscript v2.0.0 set the mainnet activation score; v2.0.1 followed. The node setup guide covers upgrades, fee policy, and changed API fields. Merged: the ZK SDK PR , which turns RISC Zero receipts into Kaspa scripts, and the sequencing-lane PR that script depends on. Both build on the public toccata branch . Testing ran on tn10-toc2 and tn10-toc3 , with covenant opcodes on TN12 separately. Activation is settled. The open checks after it are wallets, explorers, worked examples, and accepted mainnet transactions. Toccata KIPs All four read Status: Active in their raw files: KIP-16 (opcodes for verifiable computation), KIP-17 (covenants and scripting), KIP-20 (covenant IDs), KIP-21 (partitioned sequencing commitment). They moved together in one commit on 15 July 2026. The spec repo has caught up with the activation record instead of trailing it. Open KIP pull requests KIP-24 covers transaction version 1 fields and hashing. KIP-25 covers a compute budget on script execution. KIP-22 proposes a Merkle-root pay-to-script form that hides public keys until spend time. Version 1 transactions and computeBudget already run on mainnet while the KIPs specifying them are open, so cite the operator guide or the node for those two. KIP-22 has no implementation behind it. Argent argent-lang/argent is an actor-based language and compiler for covenant apps on UTXO rails. It compiles .ag source to Silverscript and portable artifacts that argent-runtime turns into transactions. Two sibling repos appeared in July: argent-playground and argent-template . Compiler and runtime exist. No release, no tag, no crates.io publish, no audit, and nothing on mainnet. The playground demos run offline against fixtures, so none of them is a deployment. vProgs The kaspanet/vprogs README describes an early-development Rust framework for based computation, with core, storage, state, scheduling, runtime, and node layers. A June merge gathered settlement covenants, batch and aggregation provers, sparse Merkle tree support, and a RISC Zero backend into master. Implementation progress on a roadmap item. Builders can study it now. Production app paths still need their own shipped evidence. DAGKnight The public dagknight branch is active, most recently promoting Universal Merge Consensus work on 14 August 2026, on top of conflict-zone and lock-removal commits from 13 August. Research and prototype evidence. Mainnet still runs GHOSTDAG, and higher block-rate claims need their own activation record. Builder tooling kaspa-python-sdk is a standalone public repo. v2.0.0 added Toccata-aligned support and the managed-wallet API for Python; v2.0.1 added get_seq_commit_lane_proof , sync progress events, and covenant-binding fixes. It ships on PyPI . Developer tooling, not protocol status. Upgrade claims still come from node, KIP, and activation evidence. Indexing PR #860 is open for review. It proposes an optional --txindex , a GetTransaction RPC path, inclusion and acceptance metadata, live updates, and pruning tied to retention-root changes. A separate relay draft explores propagating indexed data. Open, not merged. It would help wallets, explorers, and indexers once it lands. Running infrastructure? Six paths, and what each has to change Ordinary wallet users have nothing to do. Everyone below has a row. Ordinary users If you hold or send KAS from a normal wallet, there is nothing to do. Node operators Run Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer. The database upgrade only goes one way; the only path back is a resync. Wallets and submitters Use fee estimation, or update fixed-fee code to 100 sompi * max(compute grams, 2 * transaction bytes) . That floor now binds relayed transactions too, not just direct submissions. Exchanges and indexers Update SDKs or regenerate bindings, then handle transaction version 1 , storageMass , computeBudget , output covenants, and UTXO covenant_id . Miners and pools Test block templates, job distribution, solved block reconstruction, and SubmitBlock against Testnet-10. A block that strips post-Toccata fields can turn invalid after the activation score. Pool accounting Check GetBlockRewardInfo , and GetSeqCommitLaneProof where lane-proof data matters. It is the kind of detail that breaks payouts if skipped. References: Toccata node setup guide and Go Kaspad v0.12.23 . Two document series A KCC is not a KIP KIP KCC Decides Consensus and core-node behavior Conventions between independent implementations Binding on Every node that wants to stay on the network Whoever chooses to converge Adopted so far KIP-16, 17, 20 and 21 active; KIP-2 still proposed KCC-0001, KCC-0002 and KCC-0020 merged, each still Status: Draft . None accepted. The kaspanet/kccs README draws the line itself: "KCCs do not propose changes to Kaspa consensus or core-node behavior... Acceptance marks an ecosystem convergence point; it does not make the convention protocol ground truth." The live per-proposal tracker reads both repositories direct. Someone pitching you Testing a product claim built on Kaspa Protocol status is settled above. A project built on top of Kaspa is a separate question, and the answer is usually in what the pitch leaves out. Five kinds of pitch, and the signal worth trusting in each Pitch Real signal Weak signal Ask this Launchpad Issuance, a wallet flow, a liquidity path, visible holders, abuse controls. A token button and a roadmap. What can launch today, and where does the liquidity come from? DeFi Risk parameters, an oracle model, a liquidation path, an audit trail, working transactions. The word DeFi stapled to a token page. Is this mainnet, testnet evidence, or an idea riding on Toccata's name? AI agent The agent signs, pays, receives, proves work, or triggers a bounded workflow on-chain. Chatbot copy wrapped around a token. What action happens on Kaspa, and who can verify it? Wallet Clear signing, recovery, balances, history, error states, source verification. Nice screens with no transaction handling underneath. Does a normal user know what they are signing? Institutional use Custody, compliance, reporting, settlement, liquidity, support. One vague partnership post. Which institution, which requirement, and what is the evidence? This table checks whether a pitch names the parts a reviewer looks for. It does not say the product is worth building; that answer needs a named user and what they give up by switching. Next Next: Kaspa risks and open questions The strongest case against Kaspa, argued properly, and what evidence would actually prove it right.

pages.title: Kaspa Risks and Open Questions | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: The strongest case against Kaspa, argued properly: what could go wrong and what would show it going wrong.
pages.text: What could go wrong Kaspa risks and open questions The case for Kaspa is seven separate claims. Any one of them can fail while the rest hold. Seven risks, and what would settle each one Search the seven risks Verification cost Ten blocks a second raise the bandwidth, processor time, and disk a node needs. Push that far enough and only well-funded operators can still check the chain for themselves. Settled by many separate people running nodes, APIs, explorers, and indexers. Fast blocks on their own settle nothing. Security budget New coins pay the miners. That payment shrinks on a fixed schedule, and fees are not replacing it. As miner income falls, so does the cost of attacking the network. Settled by fee demand large enough to take over from new coins. Price the gap yourself below. External cost Proof-of-work security is bought with electricity, chips, and supply chains. A faster chain does not make that bill smaller. Nothing settles this one. It is the price of the security model, and it is paid every day the network runs. Liquidity Market depth, custody, and exchange support do not follow from good design. They take years, money, and legal work that has nothing to do with consensus. Settled by people able to get in and out, hold their own keys, keep books, and trade at depth. Holder counts and daily volume do not settle it. Mining concentration A few firms control ASIC Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built to do one job, in Kaspa's case running kHeavyHash, fast. It cannot be reprogrammed for anything else the way an ordinary processor can. supply. Pools cluster, and so does geography, so control can still land in few hands under a fully open protocol. Settled by block production spread across many independent payout addresses over long windows. No premine does not mean no early concentration: the fair-launch comparison plots what a fair start does and does not buy. Roadmap execution Toccata activated on mainnet. vProgs, DAGKnight, and native DeFi are separate tracks on separate timelines, and a testnet demo of one is no evidence for the rest. Settled by a mainnet release and proof it turned on, with wallets, indexers, accepted transactions, and repeat use. The status page tracks each track on its own. User demand Low fees and spare room are what apps need in order to exist. They are no proof that anyone will use one twice. Settled by people coming back because an app does the job better on Kaspa than on an ordinary server. Low fees alone do not settle it. Try it Who pays Kaspa's miners Miners sell hash power to whoever pays for it. If total pay falls, hash rate follows it down, and the cost of attacking Kaspa falls with it. How far ahead today Payments a day 82,023 Jump to Today Kaspa's busiest hour, forever Solana's traffic Fees match new coins 0.0089% of miner pay comes from fees 0.001% 0.01% 0.1% 1% 10% 100% New coins $58,358 a day Fees $5.17 a day Gap fees are 11,293x too small Reset New coins are priced at $0.0292121, the CoinGecko read behind this site's chain data on 22 August 2026, and held flat; the payout schedule itself is fixed in the protocol and steps down 5.61% a month, halving every twelve. Fees are held at the measured median of $0.000063 a payment. Source: this site's chain data , Kaspa row, read 22 August 2026. Payout schedule from rusty-kaspa's coinbase.rs subsidy table; the emission demo steps through it month by month. This deficit is not a Kaspa problem. Bitcoin has run on the same subsidy for its whole life and is still the most expensive chain in the world to attack. What is worth watching here is whether the gap closes, not that a gap exists. To price the other side of it, the attack-cost calculator puts a dollar figure on outrunning today's hash rate. What to watch How many separate node, API, and indexer operators exist. Whether roadmap items turn into apps with repeat users, since staying a demo does not count. And how fast the words live, testnet, roadmap, and research get flattened into one story in a hype cycle. For the price and hash-rate version of the same question, read Kaspa price, hash rate, and the mining cycle . Next Next: Kaspa mining Price a 51% attack on Kaspa against five other chains, and watch which half of the bill grows when it runs longer.

pages.title: Kaspa Mining | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Why Kaspa price and hash rate move on different clocks, and how to point your own ASIC at your own node.
pages.text: Proof-of-work mining Kaspa mining Price can fall while hash rate climbs. A coin market reprices in minutes; a machine market (ASIC orders, shipping, hosting, wiring) answers weeks or months later. Toccata activated at DAA score Difficulty-Adjusted Age: a running block count Kaspa consensus uses instead of wall-clock time, since many blocks land in parallel. 474,165,565, and Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the release. Nothing here is a price call. Snapshot What the network is doing KAS price Kaspa API: $0.02784831 per KAS. Coinbase all-time high: $0.2075 . Network hash rate Kaspa API: 328.1 PH/s , about 656 x i More about this comparison Compared against the 500 TH/s the Kaspa wiki records for November 29, 2022. Supply Kaspa API: 27.669B KAS mined of a 28.704B KAS maximum. Block reward Kaspa API: 2.31246515 KAS per block, the emission step that began at DAA score 504,909,000. Read from api.kaspa.org on August 29, 2026. These four numbers refresh from the same API when the page loads. The two markets The cycle What to watch Solo mining setup Sources The two markets A proof-of-work coin runs two markets on two clocks: one reprices in minutes, the other answers months later. Clocks Full loop Coin market minutes to days price, liquidity, sentiment Machine market weeks to months ASIC orders, shipping, hosting, hash rate, difficulty Hash rate can fall and still sit far above where it was a year ago. Used ASIC prices can collapse after new production overshoots demand that already cooled. Miners chase margin. Holders chase an exit or hold through it. Buyers chase a price they can stomach. ASIC makers chase order volume. The snapshot above holds a price downtrend and a multi-year hash-rate buildout at once. Coin demand Moves first Demand, liquidity, attention, and holder behavior reprice KAS within hours. Miner revenue Sets the day's math Price, block reward, fees, difficulty, and power cost decide whether mining pays that day. ASIC demand Capital follows margin Profitable mining pulls capital toward hardware orders and hosting contracts. Hash rate Arrives late ASICs ordered on a price signal can come online after that signal has already faded. Difficulty Compresses margin More machines compete for the same block reward, so each machine earns less KAS per unit of hash rate. Used machines Sort the survivors The cold phase moves hardware, coins, and conviction to whoever can outlast it. Visual shelf: market lag and miner margin Price and hash rate Divergence here is the lag working as expected, not a contradiction. Miner margin Price, block reward, fees, difficulty, hardware cost, and electricity price all land on the same miner at once. Cycle model Coins and ASICs heat and cool at different times This framing is an outside opinion, not a sourced protocol fact: an X account, @Themooseisloos5, cast the coin-and-ASIC cycle as a Carnot-engine model, four phases, borrowing the thermodynamics term for an engine that cycles between a hot and a cold state. Four phases The hot/cold cycle and Kaspa's compressed history Phase-by-phase breakdown of coin and ASIC market timing. 1 Hot coins, cold ASICs Demand moves into KAS before hardware can respond. Price rises, mining margins expand, and idle or cheap machines suddenly pencil out. 2 Hot coins, hot ASICs ASIC demand catches up. New machines get ordered, old machines get repriced upward, hash rate climbs, and early holders or miners start taking profit. 3 Cold coins, hot ASICs Price cools while machines already on order keep arriving. Difficulty can rise into a weak market, which crushes miner margins further. 4 Cold coins, cold ASICs Weak miners shut off or sell. Used machines get cheaper. Coins consolidate. The system compresses until demand, hardware, and conviction find a new balance. Kaspa compressed into one short window several discovery phases that took Bitcoin years: fair launch, fast emissions, GPU mining, an ASIC transition, exchange discovery, and price discovery all landed close together, followed by a large mining buildout. Bitcoin's early distribution, hardware maturation, exchange access, and public understanding all spread out over a much longer stretch. Compression cuts both ways. A bigger up and a bigger down both become more likely, and whether that produces a stronger base is not visible in real time. It shows up one, two, five years later, if it shows up at all. Proof of work distributes coins through hardware, electricity, and time instead of a capital-first allocation, and miners still have to cover their costs. Kaspa's fast emission schedule moves supply toward its cap quickly, which is part of the hard-money thesis. The same speed front-loads distribution pressure. Early miners earned coins by running hardware, with no allocation sold up front. That's the fair-launch case. It also means the early market absorbs a steady flow of coins moving from early miners and holders into later buyers: some take profit, some miners sell to cover power and hardware bills, some holders panic, some accumulate. Fair distribution on paper can still produce an ugly chart. Conviction usually gets tested on the downside. The upside tests it too, since rallies tempt profit-taking the same way drawdowns tempt capitulation. How this works, and the sources Kaspa's reward drops by about 5.61% (a factor of 2 to the power of −1/12) roughly every month, forever, on a schedule fixed in the software from day one. There is no single "halving day": every step is the same small size as the one before it, and the trigger is a block counter internal to the network, not the calendar. The counter is called DAA score, the network's own clock. For roughly the first six months after mainnet (Nov 2021), the reward held flat at 500 KAS per block, a bootstrap period, not part of the halving schedule. Verified in rusty-kaspa's consensus/core/src/config/params.rs : pre_deflationary_phase_base_subsidy is 500 KAS, active until deflationary_phase_daa_score 15,519,600. After that, the monthly-halving schedule took over, starting at 440 KAS per block-second, per the SUBSIDY_BY_MONTH_TABLE in consensus/src/processes/coinbase.rs . On 5 May 2025, the Crescendo hard fork moved Kaspa from 1 block per second to 10 (DAA score 110,165,000, per the v1.0.0 release notes). That split the same monthly reward across ten times as many blocks; it did not change how much is issued per month. That's why a reward chart drawn before and after Crescendo looks continuous instead of jumping. The reward right now, the total mined to date, and Kaspa's maximum supply all come from a live read of api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag and api.kaspa.org/info/coinsupply . Hardware price, power, facilities, logistics, and time push back on the buyer. An attacker needs machines built for kHeavyHash, Kaspa's proof-of-work hash function, plus electricity, facilities, cooling, firmware, logistics, and a pool or solo-mining path. Every step takes time and leaves a trail. The same specialization prices out most ordinary participants. Control settles with ASIC manufacturers, large buyers, cheap-power operators, firmware vendors, pools, and hosting sites. Used markets and more independent operators spread that control back out. A handful of dominant actors pull it in again. Proof of stake asks holders to lock the asset and follow validator rules instead. Proof of work recruits a different cast: miners carrying power bills, hosting contracts, repair costs, firmware choices, debt, and taxes, running machines that age in the real world. That friction is the security model. It is why mining behaves like an industry with payment terms, not a balance sitting quietly in a contract. Go deeper: market cap is not a pile of cash Market cap marks the whole supply at the last trade. Active float and buyer depth decide how easily that price moves. Market cap is total supply marked at the marginal price. It isn't a pool of cash sitting somewhere. A 20% price drop does not mean sellers extracted 20% of the market cap in cash. A small amount of selling can move price a long way once buyers step back. A liquidation can dump coins into market inventory that takes the market weeks or months to absorb. Sellers can keep leaning on the order book because they need liquidity before they need conviction. Market cap looks like a pool of money. Price is set at the edge, where the next buyer meets the next seller. Active float sets selloff pressure: how many coins are actually for sale, how urgent those sellers are, and how deep the buyers sit at each price rung. Total supply matters for the monetary story. Float matters in a selloff. A large liquidation keeps reshaping the market long after the candle closes, as coins move from one kind of holder into another kind of inventory. The wallet-level story needs stronger sourcing before naming actors. Go deeper: miners do not get to be pure believers A miner can believe in the network and still sell. Hardware, hosting, power, repairs, taxes, and debt create pressure a holder never faces. A holder can decide to sit still. A miner has bills: electricity, hosting, hardware debt, repairs, taxes, pool fees, upgrades. Thin margins turn a believer into a seller regardless of conviction. How the mempool actually picks, not sorts rusty-kaspa's mempool does not keep a strictly sorted fee queue. Its Frontier weighs each candidate transaction by feerate^alpha with alpha = 3 , where feerate is fee divided by mass, in sompi per gram. When total pending mass fits in one block it takes everything. When it does not, it draws a weighted random sample rather than a strict ranking, so a lower-fee transaction can get pulled in while a higher-fee one is still waiting after the draw. Transactions are also grouped into lanes by subnetwork, and once enough lanes are represented, lane assignment freezes and selection continues inside them. This demo models the feerate-weighted sampling only, not the lanes. This demo's own "picked vs. waiting" simulation approximates that principle (weighted-random draw, not the literal k·log(n) sampling algorithm or lane logic) using an illustrative, not measured, spread of other transactions' fees, since Kaspa's blocks carry too little real traffic today to have an observed fee distribution to draw from. weight(tx) = feerate(tx)^3 feerate = fee_sompi / mass_grams Source: mining/src/mempool/model/frontier.rs and mining/src/feerate/mod.rs . How the 50 GB stays flat: finality, pruning, and the discard window Why 10 blocks per second doesn't balloon the disk A pruned Kaspa node, not run with --archival (below), and not another chain. Hours since a block 6 hr kept discarded finality, 12 hr pruning, 30 hr Finality is where a reorg becomes impossible. Pruning is where a node actually throws the block away. Finality: 432,000 blocks, 12 hours Nodes refuse any reorganization that would rewrite the block. Pruning: 1,080,000 blocks, 30 hours Where a node discards old data: 648,000 blocks, 18 hours past finality. 432,000 is where the safety guarantee ends; the extra 18 hours is a deliberate margin. Full derivation below. Full vs. archival Pruning is two passes, backed by a specific proof. Archival mode, second-order pruning, and MuHash Full node vs. archival node. The behavior above is what a default node does. Anyone who wants every block kept forever runs the same rusty-kaspa software with its --archival flag. The node's own help text describes it as "an archival node: avoids deleting old block data when moving the pruning point," and attaches a plain warning: "heavy disk usage." No published size exists for a mainnet node run that way, so this page does not estimate one. First-order and second-order pruning. Pruning itself is two passes, not one. First, at the 1,080,000-block boundary above, a node discards block bodies and transactions, keeping headers. Second, deeper still, it discards most of the headers too, keeping only a sparse "posterity" chain of headers spaced about 24 hours apart back to genesis, plus a cryptographic pruning proof that lets a new node verify that sparse chain is genuine. Source: rusty-kaspa's pruning-processor code and KIP-15. MuHash: the actual answer to "is this safe." None of this works without a way to prove the current UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. set, who owns what, right now, is correct without replaying the history that produced it. MuHash is Kaspa's answer: a rolling, order-independent commitment over the UTXO set, so a node can add and remove entries as coins are created and spent and land on the same fingerprint it would get from hashing everything at once (rusty-kaspa's crypto/muhash crate). A pruned node checks each new block's UTXO commitment against that fingerprint instead of re-deriving it from years of transactions. That check, not an assumption that old data probably doesn't matter, is what makes discarding it safe. How each chain handles history The unpruned arithmetic Block count since genesis. Kaspa's mainnet genesis is timestamped November 22, 2021 (rusty-kaspa genesis.rs ). The Crescendo hard fork moved the network from one block a second to ten blocks a second on May 5, 2025, mainnet DAA score 110,165,000 (rusty-kaspa v1.0.0 release notes). That gives two eras: about 1,260 days at one block a second (108,864,000 blocks), then about 474 days at ten blocks a second through today, August 22, 2026 (409,536,000 blocks). Total: about 518,400,000 blocks ever produced. This part is measured, not estimated, aside from ordinary day-rounding. Bytes per coinbase transaction. Every block carries exactly one coinbase transaction, a structural fact, not an estimate. Its size is modeled here as a transaction header (94 bytes) plus one output (52 bytes), so 146 bytes in total, using the same byte-level constants this site's own mass calculator sources from rusty-kaspa's transaction serialization code ( consensus/core/src/mass/mod.rs , constants.rs ). This is an ESTIMATE: real coinbase transactions can carry extra payload (miner tags and similar), which this model does not include, so 146 bytes is a floor, not a measurement. The multiplication. 518,400,000 blocks × 146 bytes ≈ 75,700,000,000 bytes ≈ 76 GB. This counts only the mandatory coinbase transaction in every block. It excludes block headers, GHOSTDAG/DAG parent-pointer metadata, and every ordinary user transaction ever sent, none of which have a published per-block byte figure in this site's sources, so the real unpruned total is higher than 76 GB, and could be substantially higher. What this does and doesn't show. It shows that even the smallest, most conservative slice of unpruned growth (one mandatory transaction type, modeled at its smallest plausible size) already exceeds the actual pruned node running today, 50 GB. It does not show a growth curve over time, a total including user transactions, or a true unpruned figure, because those inputs are not sourced anywhere this site can check. No number here is invented; where an input is a genuine measurement it is labeled as such above, and where it is a model built from real but incomplete constants, it is labeled ESTIMATE. Finality and pruning depth: rusty-kaspa consensus/core/src/config/{params.rs,bps.rs,constants.rs} . FINALITY_DURATION is 43,200 seconds (12 hours); PRUNING_DURATION is 108,000 seconds (30 hours). At mainnet's ten blocks a second, finality_depth() = 432,000 blocks and pruning_depth() takes the larger of a formula (finality depth plus safety terms for merge depth and anticone/mergeset size, referencing the project's Prunality analysis ) and the flat 108,000-second floor. At ten blocks a second the flat floor wins, giving 1,080,000 blocks. No source found explains why 30 hours specifically, rather than a different round number, was chosen for that floor; it reads as a margin the protocol's authors judged sufficient rather than a value derived from a unique calculation. KIP-15 independently states the same figure in its own words: a node "prunes the transaction and header data after c. 52 hours (30 hours post-Crescendo)." Archival mode: rusty-kaspa kaspad CLI, --archival flag, help text "Run as an archival node: avoids deleting old block data when moving the pruning point (Warning: heavy disk usage)," plus --retention-period-days for partial retention. First-order and second-order pruning, and the posterity-header chain: rusty-kaspa's pruning-processor source ( consensus/src/pipeline/pruning_processor ) and KIP-15. MuHash: rusty-kaspa crypto/muhash/src/lib.rs , documented there as a rolling (homomorphic) hash supporting order-independent add_element / remove_element . Related: Kaspa mining, pruning. The setup, step by step ASIC miner Does the hashing. Its web screen asks for a pool URL, a username, and a password. → Stratum Bridge Speaks Stratum to the miner and RPC to the node. Neither one talks to the other directly. → Kaspa node Hands out block templates, and takes solved blocks back. → Kaspa network A solved block goes out to the DAG, and the reward is paid to the address in it. Your wallet address travels in the miner's username field. That is where a solo block reward lands. Shares only prove the miner is talking to the bridge. A block reward arrives when the hardware finds a valid block, and solo variance means that can take a while even on working hardware. The beginner setup One computer runs both the node and bridge. Keep two terminal windows open on that computer, then open the miner's web screen in a browser. Download the Rusty Kaspa zip for the node computer. Extract the zip and open a terminal in the folder holding the binaries. Download the sample bridge config from the repository and save it as bridge/config.yaml there. The archive does not include one. Terminal window A runs kaspad . Leave it open. Terminal window B runs stratum-bridge . Leave it open. The bridge dashboard opens at http://127.0.0.1:3030/ on the node computer. The miner points to the node computer's local IP plus port 5555 . The miner username is the Kaspa receive address plus a worker name. The dashboard should show a worker, shares, and hashrate. Keep the node, bridge, and miner on the same local network for the first setup. Do not expose RPC, dashboard, or Stratum ports to the public internet while learning.
