On macOS or Linux, open Terminal, type cd , drag the bin folder from inside the extract into Terminal, and press Enter. Run the node command for your system, and leave this window open. The bridge needs the node running continuously to fetch templates and submit blocks. Windows PowerShell Terminal window A .\kaspad.exe --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 macOS / Linux Terminal window A ./kaspad --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 Templates from an unsynced node point at stale chain state, so let sync finish before judging mining results. If a node already runs with custom flags, keep those flags and add the RPC listen setting only if the bridge can't reach the node. The official bridge docs use 127.0.0.1:16110 for the node RPC address. Step 2A Run the bridge on Windows PowerShell command, dashboard check, port check, and debug logs. Leave the node running in terminal window A. Open a second PowerShell window in the same extracted Rusty Kaspa folder. Run the bridge in external-node mode. Leave this window open too. .\stratum-bridge.exe --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external Open the dashboard in a browser on the node computer: http://127.0.0.1:3030/ To check whether the bridge is listening on port 5555 : netstat -ano | findstr :5555 To turn on more detailed bridge logs before starting it: $env:RUST_LOG="info,kaspa_stratum_bridge=debug" "Cannot find bridge/config.yaml" means the config was never downloaded, since the release archive does not ship one. A dashboard that won't open points the same way: the bridge falls back to code defaults when it finds no config, and those defaults leave the dashboard switched off. Check the last few lines printed in terminal window B. Step 2B Run the bridge on macOS or Linux Terminal command, dashboard check, port check, and debug logs. Leave the node running in terminal window A. Open a second Terminal window in the same extracted Rusty Kaspa folder. If needed, allow the binary to run. Run the bridge in external-node mode. Leave this window open too. chmod +x ./stratum-bridge ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external Open the dashboard in a browser on the node computer: http://127.0.0.1:3030/ To check whether the bridge is listening on port 5555 : lsof -i :5555 To turn on more detailed bridge logs for one run: RUST_LOG="info,kaspa_stratum_bridge=debug" ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external On macOS, Gatekeeper may ask for approval before it runs a downloaded binary. Only approve binaries pulled from the official Rusty Kaspa release page. Other route If the bridge should start its own node In-process mode from the official bridge docs. In-process mode, also documented by the bridge, starts kaspad inside the same process as the bridge. It does not run as a separate program. Windows PowerShell Bridge plus in-process node .\stratum-bridge.exe --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode inprocess -- --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 macOS / Linux Bridge plus in-process node ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode inprocess -- --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 The -- separator is not optional. Bridge flags go before it, node flags after. Steps 3 and 4 Find the local IP, then point the ASIC IP lookup, then the miner's pool fields. Step 3. Find the node computer's local IP address The miner needs the local network address of the computer running the bridge, usually something like 192.168.x.x or 10.0.x.x . Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt ipconfig Look for the active Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter and copy the IPv4 Address. macOS Wi-Fi ipconfig getifaddr en0 If Ethernet is active, System Settings can be easier: Network, then your active connection, then Details. Linux Terminal hostname -I Use the address on the same network as your miner. Step 4. Point the ASIC at the bridge Open the miner's web screen. If you don't know the miner's IP address, check your router's connected-device list or the manufacturer's setup tool. Type the miner IP into a browser, sign in, and find the mining or pool configuration page. Use the bridge computer's local IP address and one of the Stratum ports from the sample config, starting with port 5555 . Miner field Put this in Example Pool URL <node-computer-ip>:5555 192.168.1.10:5555 Username / worker kaspa:YOUR_WALLET_ADDRESS.WORKERNAME kaspa:kaspa:qq...abcd.ks0 Password Use the miner UI default if it requires a value. x is common in miner UIs, but the Rusty Kaspa bridge docs define only pool URL and username. A Kaspa address already starts with kaspa: , so the username field ends up looking like kaspa:kaspa:... . That duplication matches the official bridge format; it's not a typo. Some miner screens expect a URL prefix instead. The official bridge docs give the pool URL as <your_pc_IPv4>:<stratum_port> ; if a miner rejects that format, check its manual for the exact Stratum URL syntax it wants. Step 5 Check that it's working Bridge window, dashboard, miner screen, and node checks. Bridge window Should keep running and show miner connection or job activity. Dashboard Open http://127.0.0.1:3030/ and look for active workers, shares, hashrate, and recent activity. Miner screen Should show an active pool, accepted shares, and hashrate. Node Should stay synced and keep receiving network updates. Accepted shares confirm the setup is wired correctly. They are not the reward event: a found block is. A correctly configured rig can run for a long stretch with steady shares and zero blocks. That is solo variance. Reference Miner brands What changes by miner or software type? IceRiver, Bitmain, BzMiner, Goldshell, and field-name differences. The bridge detects several miner and mining-software types automatically and adjusts protocol handling per type. The setup screen itself still belongs to the miner manufacturer, so field labels vary. The bridge docs list two job formats, and every supported device falls into one of them. Extranonce, single hex string IceRiver, BzMiner, and Goldshell. No extranonce, array plus timestamp Bitmain and GodMiner. Whatever the brand, the fields that matter stay the same: pool URL, username or wallet field, and a password only if the miner UI demands one. Ports Pick the first port Start with 5555; lower ports are for troubleshooting. The sample config exposes several Stratum ports, each tuned to a different worker difficulty. Start with 5555 . Drop to a lower-difficulty port only when troubleshooting a connection or matching a weaker worker per the bridge docs. Port Sample config purpose 5559 Low-difficulty workers. 5560 Low-difficulty workers. 5561 Medium-difficulty workers. 5555 Higher-difficulty workers. Start here for a normal ASIC setup. 5556 , 5557 , 5558 Higher difficulty ports. Toccata Toccata mining checks Version, activation record, post-Toccata template fields, and testnet checks. Post-activation block templates can carry new transaction fields. The official node guide warns pools and custom mining stacks to preserve those fields all the way from block template to solved block submission, or risk submitting an invalid block. Upgrade Use Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer for the node and bridge path. Activation record Mainnet activation crossed DAA score 474,165,565 . Check the status page for post-activation checks. Template fields Custom mining software must preserve post-Toccata fields: transaction version, storage mass, compute budget, and covenant outputs. Test first Run it on Testnet-10 where possible before trusting a mainnet mining path built after the activation score. Fixes If it doesn't connect Pool dead, empty dashboard, RPC, firewall, and rewards. Symptom Check Miner says pool dead Use the node computer's local IP address. 127.0.0.1 points the miner back at itself. Dashboard is empty Check the bridge is still running, the miner is on the same network, and the pool URL uses a port from the sample config. Bridge cannot reach node Confirm the node is running with RPC at 127.0.0.1:16110 , or update the bridge config to the node's actual RPC address. Firewall blocks connection Allow the Stratum port on the node computer for the local network. No rewards Check shares first. Rewards need a solved block, and solo variance can leave a working rig without one for a long time. Toccata activation day Recheck versions and logs. Past the activation score, a block that strips new fields is invalid. Network exposure Keep node RPC, the bridge dashboard, and Stratum ports on the local network while learning. Wallet safety Use a public Kaspa receive address for the miner username. Never paste a seed phrase or private key into miner, bridge, or dashboard settings. Sources Sources, with what each backs Open the table: bridge docs, node guides, and public APIs Source Used for Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge docs Beta status, external-node mode, in-process mode, dashboard, ports, miner setup, and username format. Sample bridge config The file to download, since the release archives do not carry one. It sets the dashboard port, the Stratum ports, and the node RPC address. Toccata node setup guide v2.0.1 upgrade guidance, miner and pool checks, fee policy, and post-Toccata field preservation. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 release The Windows, macOS, and Linux archives used in this guide. Kaspa public API: blockDAG state The mainnet DAA and network read behind the snapshot above. Kaspa public API: coin supply and block reward The supply and reward figures in the snapshot above. Kaspa public API: network hash rate The hash-rate reading in the snapshot above. Kaspa wiki timeline Early hash-rate milestones: 60 MH/s in November 2021, 10 TH/s in June 2022, 50 TH/s in August 2022, and 500 TH/s in November 2022. Kaspa wiki tokenomics Fair-launch and no-premine context. Coinbase Kaspa price page All-time-high reference and market-data context. CoinGecko Kaspa page and CoinGecko API Dated current price read. Kaspa Explained status page Activation tracked separately from the setup instructions. The coin-and-ASIC cycle framing is credited to @Themooseisloos5's X posts. Price, hash-rate, supply, and protocol-status claims use the sources listed above. Next Next: Build Kaspa apps Try to break a Toccata covenant vault yourself, and see exactly which attack gets stopped and why.

pages.title: Build on Kaspa: Toccata App Ideas and Builder Paths | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Three ways to build on Kaspa, and how to work out which one your idea needs.
pages.text: Build on Kaspa Build Kaspa apps Spend limits, escrow paths, asset rules, and proof checks now live in Kaspa's own script, where anyone can read them before money moves. Toccata put them on mainnet at DAA score 474,165,565. Status, and where to check a product claim before pitching it Status: read how covenants work for the plain-language version of what activated, and try breaking one below. Before pitching: run product claims through Status , and adoption risk through Risks . Pick a route What to build Run the checks Route Pick the route Plenty of Kaspa products need only payments, receipts, or better wallet UX. Toccata matters only when the product needs a spend rule the user can read before funds move. If Kaspa's fit isn't obvious yet, check which jobs gain from Kaspa . Two questions before the table: name the action, then say why a server can't do it instead 1 / Job Name the action Send, receive, lock, refund, issue, replay, prove, or settle: one verb, one person doing it often enough to care. 2 / Reason Say why a server can't do it instead Self-custody, public ordering, or proof that state wasn't rewritten in private. One has to be true. What the app needs Route Why that one Payment, receipt, balance, withdrawal, or support evidence Live network work Current wallets, APIs, and accepted-transaction checks already handle this. Vault, escrow, spend cap, asset rule, release, refund, or timeout Toccata covenants A bounded spend rule is simpler to build and audit than a full app runtime. When to split into more than one covenant If the product splits into states that never touch, use one covenant per state and the parallel work comes free. One app keeps its own richer state from accepted Kaspa transactions Based app or replay path The app proves or replays its own state without needing cross-app atomicity. Each action needs its own proof, privacy check, or custom validity rule Inline ZK It fits, and costs more proof and ops work than covenants or based apps do. The claim depends on another chain, an oracle, a price, or a real-world event Inline ZK, plus an anchor A proof checks its own inputs, never the world. Name the anchor first: source root, finality certificate, oracle, or challenge process. Many users mutate the same app state at once Future full vProgs Build the narrow app first. Argent's Inter-Covenant Communication Separately compiled covenant apps joined into one all-or-nothing transaction. already runs separate covenant apps as one, in unaudited offline demos. Start a based app as deterministic replay of accepted transactions, and add ZK only once proofs, privacy, or bridge logic become the product edge. A fungible token means building against KCC-0020 A Kaspa Call for Conventions: an agreement between wallets and apps on a shared format, like a token standard. It is not a consensus change; a KIP is. , a draft standard with a known supply-split defect. Detail on the KIP and KCC page . A covenant can only inspect the transaction spending it. It has no shared-state read into the wider chain. Why there's no shared-state read, and who's already hit it Reading shared on-chain state, a price, a pool balance, consumes it in the same breath. Kaspa has no reference-input equivalent to Cardano, Ergo, or CKB. A builder raised the gap in the Kaspa Core R&D Telegram group on 18 July 2026, sketching a covenant DEX that needs a shared price board. Six reactions, no reply. No KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. yet says whether the fix belongs at L1 or in a future vProg. Try it Attack a covenant vault Before writing spend-rule code, see what a covenant actually blocks. A worked example. Nothing here is on a real blockchain. This vault holds 10,000 KAS behind four rules. Get any of it to an address you control without satisfying all four. Status: the enforcement is live on mainnet; the rule's own notation is illustrative. i Which parts are live and which are notation only The cap, destination and delay run on mainnet via KIP-17 and KIP-20 . The rule below is written in Argent's syntax, which is still research. Attempt Vault details & rules Try to get money out of the vault Start from one of these, or set up your own attempt. Direct attempts, each breaks one rule on purpose Take it all right now Withdraw before the wait is up Send it to my own address Trigger recovery, then redirect it Break no rule at all Withdraw the max, hour after hour How you're trying to get it out Normal withdrawal Emergency recovery Amount to withdraw (KAS) Where the money goes The vault's own payout address The vault's own recovery address An address you control, not the vault's Time since the vault's last withdrawal (DAA score, Kaspa's block counter) ≈ 60 minutes Send it Start over Attempts so far # Attempt Amount Sent to Result Vault state (made up, for this example) What the covenant enforces Who can sign A withdrawal needs the owner's signature. Recovery needs the recovery key instead. No other key works. What can leave A withdrawal moves at most 500 KAS, and only to the vault's fixed payout address. Recovery empties the vault instead, and only to the fixed recovery address. What comes next Every withdrawal must recreate the vault with the same KIP-20 covenant ID and the updated balance and last-spend score. A transaction that doesn't is spending a lookalike, not the vault. How soon again A withdrawal must wait 36,000 DAA score since the vault's last spend (roughly one hour at 10 blocks per second) before it is valid again. Rule definitions and sources state VaultState { byte[32] owner_pk_hash; byte[32] recovery_pk_hash; byte[32] payout_spk_hash; byte[32] recovery_spk_hash; int balance; int last_spend_daa; } actor Vault owns VaultState { entry withdraw(int amount, sig owner_sig, pubkey owner_pk) emits next: Vault { require(blake2b(owner_pk) == owner_pk_hash); require(checkSig(owner_sig, owner_pk)); // what can leave: fixed cap, fixed destination require(amount <= 500 && amount <= balance); require(tx.outputSpkHash(0) == payout_spk_hash); require(tx.outputAmount(0) == amount); // how soon again: time since this covenant's own last spend require(tx.inputDaaScore(self) - last_spend_daa >= 36000); // what comes next: same KIP-20 covenant id, updated state VaultState new_state = { owner_pk_hash: owner_pk_hash, recovery_pk_hash: recovery_pk_hash, payout_spk_hash: payout_spk_hash, recovery_spk_hash: recovery_spk_hash, balance: balance - amount, last_spend_daa: tx.inputDaaScore(self), }; become next <- Vault(new_state); } entry recover(sig recovery_sig, pubkey recovery_pk) { require(blake2b(recovery_pk) == recovery_pk_hash); require(checkSig(recovery_sig, recovery_pk)); // no cap, no delay: recovery ignores both // but the destination is still fixed, and the vault ends require(tx.outputSpkHash(0) == recovery_spk_hash); require(tx.outputAmount(0) == balance); // no `become`: this covenant's lineage ends here } } Pseudocode in Argent's actor/entry/require/become style, a proposed Kaspa contract language still in research; see Argent and Silverscript, explained for that project's status. Introspection opcodes named against the primitives KIP-17 actually defines: OpTxOutputAmount , OpTxOutputSpk , OpTxInputDaaScore , OpTxLockTime . KIP-17 and its continuation-identity companion KIP-20 are both live on mainnet as of Toccata. A spend either carries the same covenant_id as the UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. it consumes, or proves a fresh one through the genesis hash, so a forged lookalike cannot claim an existing covenant's identity. Evidence How much of this is actually running A third-party indexer counts 38,332 covenants ever created on mainnet, 673 still active, holding about 1,566,585 KAS. Testnet-10 carries far more test activity, about 86,376 active. Use case What the rule controls Status Vault Withdrawal delay, recovery key, spend cap, or escape path. Live Escrow Release, refund, timeout, or dispute transition. Live Assurance funding Payout only after enough matching commitments arrive before a deadline. Live Controlled assets Transfer rules, controller input, or issuer rule. Live ZK proof checks A claim about chosen public inputs. Live Cross-app composition Several app states succeed or fail together in one transaction. Demos only Shared mutable state Many users mutating one app state at once. Roadmap Baseline written into this page August 29, 2026. The rule for assurance funding runs live today. A shipped coordination-market product does not: that's still a research direction, and a covenant can't see an outside price or event without a named oracle. Primary sources: KIP-17 covenants and KIP-20 covenant IDs . Raw text, all reading Status: Active : KIP-16 , KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-21 . Try it What a proof can and can't verify KIP-16's proof check confirms a proof is valid. It says nothing about where its inputs came from, and that gap is where a real integration goes wrong. A secret number Today's real BTC price Price + an oracle Run the checks again Ask a centralized server Check the proof yourself Why this happens, and how it maps to Kaspa Kaspa's Toccata hard fork added OpZkPrecompile (KIP-16, Status: Active), an opcode that checks a proof against a chosen proof system, initially Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct. The opcode confirms a proof verifies against a given verifying key and public inputs. It says nothing about where those public inputs came from. Proving "I know a secret number" is exactly that kind of self-contained check: everything the proof needs is already in its own inputs. Proving "the real price of BTC right now" asks the proof to vouch for a fact about the outside world, which no arithmetic check can do by itself. That needs an external anchor: a light client, a finality certificate, or a reporter set with something to lose. The reason this beats asking a server the same yes/no question: a server's answer is only as good as your trust in that server, and checking it means taking its word or getting access to the private data behind it. A verified proof is checked against Kaspa's own public ledger, by anyone, using only the verifying key and the public inputs already on that ledger. Nothing about the app's private state has to be exposed for the check to work. So how does a fact from outside the chain, a price, a bridge event, a sports score, get into a proof's public inputs? Someone has to attest to it: sign a statement saying "this is the value," and hand the app that signature instead of the raw fact. The proof then checks the signature the way it checks any other public input. That is an oracle. It is not a cryptographic trick that removes the trust problem; it is a trust decision: pick a signer, and believe them. Kaspa's L1 does not ship an oracle system. KIP-16 (Status: Active) added the verifier opcode, wired to Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct. Which oracle to trust, how many signers to require, and what happens when they disagree are application choices, not protocol ones. Whether that arrangement is trustworthy is a question about the signer, never one the on-chain math can answer. Kaspa's ten blocks a second means a signed attestation lands on-chain and starts accumulating proof-of-work in about a second, rather than waiting on a slower chain's block time. That shortens how long an app sits on stale data. It does not touch who you are trusting. A faster chain gets you a wrong price faster, exactly as easily as a right one. Sources: KIP-16, OpZkPrecompile , docs.kaspa.org/programmability . No proof is actually computed here; this toy names what a proof would and would not cover, and no network requests are made. What to build Products, sorted by what they need Six that need only the live network They already have users. Receipts and checkout Invoices, tips, and withdrawals showing inclusion, confidence, and risk as three separate facts. Self-custody tools Address books, payment requests, and accounting exports for keys people hold themselves. Support helpers Splitting exchange delay from network delay, which is what most support tickets mix up. Node and API monitors Diff a public API against your own node, and flag a stale provider before users notice. Proof pages One page carrying user action, txid, source, status label, and current blocker. Activity dashboards Payments, mining, and spam pulled apart, so one raw count stops passing for a signal. The hard part is the gap between a good interface and a rule the network enforces: address generation, a synced node, Silverscript A higher-level language that compiles down to Kaspa script, so a covenant can be written as readable rules instead of hand-assembled opcodes. compilation, and explorer-visible outputs all have to work first. No getUtxosByCovenantId RPC exists yet, so every covenant project ships its own indexer. Six more that need a spend rule Vault policies Spend caps, delayed withdrawal, and a recovery key, enforced by the spend script itself. Assurance funding Funds release only once enough backers commit by the deadline. Miss it and refunds fire on their own. Conditional escrow Milestone payments, disputes, and refund paths, each step visible on-chain. Controlled assets Tickets, credentials, and redeemable claims, each with a transfer rule the holder can read. Atomic market primitives Swaps, auctions, and OTC flows, with script behavior staying bounded. Games and state machines Turn-based apps where player state, move routing, and settlement are separate steps. Attach a user job to every build: a budget nobody can drain at once, an asset that moves only under a controller rule. Small covenant-shaped products come first, and based-app paths only once the product needs shared state. A product that signs transactions, holds funds, or promises uptime needs a node, an indexer, and a backup provider, not one hosted API. Advanced state-transition proof note State-transition proof models follow one pattern: selected-parent root plus current root plus leaf write witnesses. That keeps validation local to the single transition. Clients never have to maintain the whole incremental SMT. To place a specific public claim in one lane before posting it, use the claim fact-check . Node, wallet, and exchange Toccata prep work is in the status operator checklist . Verify yourself Run the checks yourself A wallet screen shows a balance and asks to be believed. Climb the ladder when the situation calls for it: an explorer read, a second API, then a node answering from chain state. A normal payment doesn't need every rung. Mainnet commands change with releases, so check the source links before touching real funds. Setup commands for all three routes: run your own node, TN12 testnet, or a hosted API Run a node TN12 testnet Hosted API Run a Rusty Kaspa node Docker for the container route, Rust and Cargo for the source route. A node verifies chain state. It does not create or protect wallet keys. docker pull kaspanet/rusty-kaspad:latest mkdir -p ~/kaspa-data docker run -d --name kaspa-node --restart unless-stopped \ -v ~/kaspa-data:/app/data \ -p 16110:16110 -p 16111:16111 -p 17110:17110 -p 18110:18110 \ kaspanet/rusty-kaspad:latest docker ps docker logs --tail=80 kaspa-node Source build, then the same node with UTXO indexing: git clone https://github.com/kaspanet/rusty-kaspa cd rusty-kaspa cargo run --release --bin kaspad cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --utxoindex Use --utxoindex when wallet or UTXO queries need indexed state. A node that hasn't finished syncing answers confidently and wrongly, so wait for sync. Open the terminal wallet and RPC path The terminal RPC and wallet runtime, from a checkout: cd cli cargo run --release For every transaction read the address, amount, fee, and network before signing. Send a tiny amount first, then confirm the accepted txid through an independent source. Enable a JSON WebSocket RPC endpoint wRPC is off by default. It opens a WebSocket SDKs can query for node state, so bind it carefully on public machines: cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --utxoindex --rpclisten-json=default Practice on testnet, then in the TN12 lab cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --testnet cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --testnet --netsuffix=10 --utxoindex Check the current netsuffix, release, and flags against active docs first. The TN10 examples are Crescendo-era context; the Rusty Kaspa tn10-toc2 and tn10-toc3 pre-releases, plus the Testnet-10 REST status endpoint, are the Testnet-10 Toccata activation evidence. TN12 is where covenant and replay experiments get tested before mainnet. The lab repo ships a results explorer and a playground : git clone https://github.com/parker2017code/tn12-covenant-vault-demo cd tn12-covenant-vault-demo npm ci npm run check:all npm run check:tn12 Fund only the printed kaspatest: addresses, from a faucet that serves testnet-12. Every Kaspa testnet shares that prefix, so tKAS from a Testnet-10 faucet lands on a network TN12 never sees. Anything run with --submit broadcasts for real. Hosted API checks The Kaspa Developer Platform is a hosted API for chain data, transaction checks, and a node RPC proxy. It works for prototypes, dashboards, and second-source checks. It is not a protocol source. POST Transaction acceptance Batch-check txids for acceptance, block hash, and confirmation count. curl --request POST \ --url https://api.kas.fyi/v1/transactions/acceptance \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' \ --data '{"transactionIds":["<txid>"]}' GET DAA-score blocks Read a bounded DAA-score range. KDP caps each request at 100 scores. curl --request GET \ --url https://api.kas.fyi/v1/blocks/daa-score/{daa_score_start}/{daa_score_end} \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' GET Address history Large histories need cursor pagination. Cache results, or the requests pile up fast. curl --request GET \ --url 'https://api.kas.fyi/v1/addresses/<address>/transactions?limit=100' \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' DATA API data rules Amounts arrive as sompi strings. The key goes in x-api-key , and a 429 means back off. 1 KAS = 100000000 SOMPI amount: "31112708372" The community REST API at api-tn10.kaspa.org is a separate trap. Its submit schema never carried compute_budget , checked against the live openapi.json . Silverscript covenant deployments through it fail with "script units exceeded the amount committed in the input: used=100000, limit=9999." Submit straight to a kaspad node instead. Kaspa Developer Platform reference: index , llms.txt , transaction acceptance , DAA-score blocks , blue-score ranges , data types , and rate limits . The mainnet REST API and docs.kaspa.org references are separate, unauthenticated sources for the same kind of data. Checks that catch the expensive mistakes Pick network first. Mainnet uses kaspa: , TN12 uses kaspatest: , and reusing test keys for mainnet is how funds get lost. Use the right node. Testnet covenant work needs a build for that testnet. Mainnet builders run the released mainnet node. Check sync and UTXO index. An unsynced node or a missing index returns a balance that looks real and isn't. Separate UI policy from consensus rules. A wallet warning is not an enforced covenant. The chain doesn't know the UI exists. Record exact submit details. Log SDK version, node version, network id, endpoint, encoding, and tx version every time. After submit, fetch accepted state and diff it against what the app claims happened. If they don't match, that's the bug report. Three results get read as the same result and are not: a transaction the network accepted, a local reject inside one machine's script engine, and a wallet-policy refusal the network never saw. Open verification checklist Builder habit Consequence Check Fetch accepted state after submit Local construction proves a transaction was built. It doesn't prove the network accepted it. Record is_accepted , accepting block data, output script type, address, and amount. Pin the submit surface REST, JSON wRPC, Borsh wRPC, SDK versions, and testnet branches can each hand back a different transaction shape for the same request. Log SDK version, node version, network id, endpoint, encoding, tx version, and input budget fields. Compare with a known working spend Witness order, signature preimage, redeem-script shape, and constructor keys are far easier to debug against a sibling transaction that already worked than in isolation. Diff the failing path against an accepted release, refund, or simple payment path before blaming protocol rules. Label failed attempts narrowly A tooling failure and a consensus failure look identical from the outside. They need different labels or the next builder repeats your mistake. Keep the artifact, but mark it as bad config, stale tooling, submit mismatch, or confirmed consensus rejection. A prototype stays testnet-only until mainnet evidence says otherwise. References What to read before writing code Docs, SDK references, source repos, and community infrastructure Kaspa docs , especially Getting started , Programmability , Transaction payload , Accepted transactions , and Kaspa node . Izio's programmability overview lays out the same decision tree in more depth: covenants , based apps , inline ZK , and full vProgs ; KASmedia's fast-PoW recap covers the same ground for a less technical reader. Aspectron RpcClient docs , signTransaction docs , submit-transaction request docs , and worked WASM examples define the JavaScript SDK request shape. rusty-kaspa TN12 branch , Toccata branch , Silverscript , TN12 faucet , the Testnet-10 faucet , and the TN12 explorer , all separate from the v2.0.1 activation evidence. RPC port reference and the public node network cover how to reach a node directly. Michael Sutton A core Kaspa developer who led the Rust rewrite and much of 2026's covenant and scripting work, including Argent and Silverscript. 's vProgs masterclass covers app-to-app composition and prover incentives. The code and the design notes sit apart from it: the kaspanet/vprogs repo and its RISC0 backend commit , two gists, covenant++ and STARK blocks , and the based-ZK-rollup work at research.kas.pa . Node and community infrastructure a builder is likely to touch. To run and index: the official rusty-kaspad Docker image , simply-kaspa-indexer , the DNS seeder , and kHost . To build and sign: the kaspa-js library, and two signing tools that track the Python SDK, KasSigner and KasSee . To read the codebase: an AI-generated DeepWiki . Design discussion runs ahead of any KIP in the Core R&D Telegram group . Kaspa Explained status and the source hierarchy hold the live/targeted/roadmap/research boundaries. pages.title: Argent and Silverscript, Explained | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Argent compiles covenant applications down to Silverscript. Here is the language model, a worked example, what the README actually says, and the repository signals.
pages.text: Application layer Argent and Silverscript, explained Toccata made covenants A rule attached to a coin. The network itself checks it on every spend, not a server's promise. enforceable. Argent, Michael Sutton's compiler, turns a readable application description into the Silverscript the network already checks. Status: unaudited, pre-release. Try it One line at a time, from Argent down to Kaspa Script Nothing reaches the network as Argent. Every line has to end up as script a Kaspa node already knows how to check. Argent’s own Ticket example hands a ticket to a new owner in three lines. Pick one and follow it down. Ownership check Signature check Next coin Argent · .ag Silverscript · .sil Kaspa Script not published A Kaspa node never sees the top two rows. Only the bottom one runs, so only the bottom one decides whether the money moves. Argent lines quoted from the argent-lang/argent README. Silverscript builtins documented in Silverscript's tutorial . What's real here, and what's illustrative The Argent lines are quoted from the Ticket transfer entry and from Argent's own README. The full listing is below, in the language model section. Argent, Silverscript, and Kaspa Script all use require . blake2b and checkSig are Silverscript builtins, documented in its tutorial with the identical call shape Argent uses, so Argent inherits those expressions rather than reinventing them. The become line is different. Argent's README says become routes "lower to output validation," and that an exact continuation into the same actor "can use cheaper script-public-key checks." Silverscript's own tutorial documents the named builtin for that job: validateOutputState(int outputIndex, object newState) used to "validate continuation into the same contract template." The Silverscript line shown for that step names this real, documented builtin and shapes it around the Ticket example's own fields. It is not a copy of Argent's actual generated .sil output for this contract, which neither repository publishes. Past Silverscript, compilation reaches Kaspa Script. silverc 's own docs describe its compiled JSON output as carrying a bytecode field, "the compiled bytecode (as an array of bytes)." No file in either repository disassembles that array into opcode names for a real example, so this demo does not invent one. The gap it fills A covenant is opcodes. An application is several agreeing. A covenant is a rule attached to a coin , written as raw opcodes. One coin with one rule is readable. An application is several of them that have to agree, and few teams can audit that by hand. Argent is Michael Sutton's answer, not an official protocol project. You describe an actor, a coin that carries state and the rules for spending it, and the compiler writes the script. Inter-Covenant Communication Separately compiled covenant apps joined into one all-or-nothing transaction: either every part lands, or none does. lets an actor in one compiled app authorize an actor in another, inside a single transaction, so two apps built separately land together or not at all. It is the second of three rungs on the UTXO page , and the first that is not live. Open the language model and a worked example On an account chain, a contract sits at an address and receives calls. On Kaspa there is no such thing to call. There are only outputs, and a covenant is a rule about what the next output has to look like. Argent takes that constraint seriously instead of hiding it. Four ideas carry the core, and they are not the whole surface: the documented set is eight, adding delegate , consumes , and emits , with the route machinery sitting behind those. A state is a typed record. An actor owns one. An entry is a way to spend that actor, taking arguments and declaring which actors it emits. And become names the successor the transaction creates. state TicketState { byte[32] owner; int units; } actor Ticket owns TicketState { entry transfer(byte[32] next_owner, sig owner_sig, pubkey owner_pk) emits next: Ticket { require(blake2b(owner_pk) == owner); require(checkSig(owner_sig, owner_pk)); require(next.value == self.value); TicketState new_state = { owner: next_owner, units: units, }; become next <- Ticket(new_state); } } app Tickets { actor Ticket; } Nothing here is a call to a contract. The transaction spends the old ticket and creates the new one, and every require is a condition the script engine checks before it will let that happen. If a condition fails, the transaction is invalid. There is no revert, no gas refund, and no partially applied state, because there was never a running program to interrupt. What the compiler outputs The compiler emits three things for each build, and every one is inspectable without rebuilding the project: artifact.json as the portable description, manifest.json as build metadata, and the rest as ordinary .sil Silverscript contracts. Those contracts use no covenant macros and compile like any other Silverscript, which matters for review: an auditor reads generated script, not a black box. An argentc inspect command reports script and state sizes, static opcode counts, entry arguments, route metadata, and signature-script size estimates, without rebuilding. The design targets script composition primitives such as OP_CAT and OP_SUBSTR , transaction introspection, and the consensus-supported covenant identities of KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. -20, the piece Toccata carried to mainnet. Repository signals Three active repos, zero releases A release tag is what a build gets pinned to. Argent has none, and the Silverscript audit it is waiting on has not finished either. Repository Created Last push Stars Releases argent 2026-06-16 2026-08-27 22 None argent-playground 2026-07-09 2026-08-26 7 None argent-template 2026-07-24 2026-08-25 8 None Baseline read from GitHub on August 29, 2026. What's proven, what isn't Partitioned state works. Shared state is a design direction. Shape of the state What Argent has for it One coin per thing Every published example: one UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. per ticket, per game, per position. One state, many writers Nothing public. That shape is most of what people mean by DeFi. The README carries a caution and a list of working pieces. Quote one half without the other and you get the project wrong. Either way, nothing built with Argent runs on Kaspa mainnet today. Open the evidence: the DEX example, commit history, and the README quoted in full The playground's DEX is a single pair, and the compiler's own SECURITY.md never mentions replicas, keepers, or bounded divergence, the shape a partitioned pool would need. Three repositories, and one person writes nearly all of it. As of mid-August, Michael Sutton held 73 of the compiler's 77 commits, and 58 of those landed in July, when the project moved out of his personal namespace into an argent-lang organization. The compiler reached 80 commits by August 24, 2026, all of them syncing generated output with Silverscript's own changes. The per-author split was not rerun at that count. The README's caution is real: "The project is still under active development and is not yet release-ready," a production path opens only "Once Silverscript completes its audit and is released," and Argent "will still need further audit and hardening before general production use." The second half names what that caution is about: "The main pieces are present: compiler, generated Silverscript, portable artifacts, runtime transaction building, multi-actor routing, cross-app linking," and five more. That is a list of things that work, not things planned. The gate is a review queue, not a construction site: an audit on Silverscript, then a release, then an audit on Argent. Until then the README points at advanced users who can read the generated .sil themselves. Silverscript recommends its bytecode artifact only on testnet-10. Kaspa's Argent chapter is more cautious again, calling it "a design direction and prototype, not a production-stable API." That reads as the ecosystem's conservative floor, not the project's current state: Kaspa's own chapter still links the old repository path. Sources Sources, with what each backs argent-lang/argent : the compiler, the Ticket example above, the commit history, and every status sentence here. argent-playground : the single-pair DEX example, and the absence of a shared-state one. argent-template : the starter project, third of the repos in the table. kaspanet/silverscript and its tutorial : that blake2b , checkSig and validateOutputState are builtins, called the way Argent calls them. Kaspa's own Argent chapter : "a design direction and prototype, not a production-stable API." KIP-20 : covenant IDs, the consensus feature the compiler targets. Active since Toccata.
